title: ACT Greens end key working relationship with government
text:
The ACT Greens have ended their agreement to support the government on key votes, citing a breakdown in negotiations over priority issues.

ACT Greens leader Jo Clay said the end of the agreement with Labor would apply for the remainder of the parliamentary term.

Ms Clay said the move was the decision of all four Greens MLAs as well as party members, who were consulted.

She said the ending of a formal relationship allowed the party to better hold ACT Labor to account, and that she had informed Chief Minister Andrew Barr of the decision earlier in the day.

While the party did not renew its coalition with Labor after the 2024 election, they did agree to the confidence and supply agreement, which helps the minority Labor government pass legislation through the ACT Legislative Assembly.

"When negotiations began in early August, the Greens' goal was simple: secure the best possible outcomes for Canberrans, the climate, and environment," Ms Clay said.

"This means measurable progress on public housing, stronger protections for renters, protecting the Western Edge, and properly resourced community services like our libraries."

The end of the formal working agreement leaves ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr's minority government in a perilous position. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Ms Clay said the government was going to have to be "very careful, issue by issue to work with everyone in parliament" from now on.

She said the party had set a "clear, fair bar" for the government but it had chosen "not to be accountable in delivering their own policy".

The ACT Greens have been playing the hokey pokey, but now they are out Ruling out forming a new coalition government with Labor could allow the ACT Greens to reset their priorities.

"We asked for reasonable outcomes with dates attached. But what we got in return was non-commitment," she said.

"As we've seen very recently, from the cancelled ice rink in Tuggeranong, to below-inflation pay offers for teachers, to cut library hours, the community is tired of good intentions with no follow-through."

But she said they would help the upcoming budget pass through the Assembly.

"We went in to negotiate on this budget earlier this year and we got some really key concessions in there. We made sure that the health levy would not be coming back, we made sure that we got a proper uplift in community sector funding," she said.

"This budget is not perfect, but this budget is a budget that the Greens will support passage of."

Ms Clay said the party was not considering forming government with the Liberals at this stage.

Gambling, horse racing and climate change all issues

A list provided by the Greens of commitments it said the government had "refused" to deliver on also included harm-reduction on gambling, funding for the horse-racing industry and climate change.

The list added that the party had wanted to see a "clear action plan to phase out petrol and diesel transport, despite the current fuel crisis hitting Canberrans' back pockets, and Labor's own commitment to phase out by 2035".

title: NRLW greats Elliot, Baxter, announce retirement at end of finals
text:
The NRLW will farewell two of its most influential figures with Sydney Roosters pair Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter announcing their retirements.

Elliott and Baxter confirmed on Wednesday that this NRLW season would be their last, leaving the duo on track to go out with another premiership at the Roosters.

Elliott's decision to call it a day is a shock.

She is 28 and hopes to play for Australia at the end-of-year World Cup, but after having a child last year the front-rower wants to prioritise a growing family.

An emotional Baxter said on Thursday she had made the call after returning from last year's ACL rupture.

Corban Baxter was among the Roosters' foundation players. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The 32-year-old has still starred for the Roosters at fullback, but felt her body was finding it hard to keep up with the demands.

Both have been stars of the NRLW since its second season in 2019, with Baxter missing the opening four-week competition through a shoulder injury.

Elliott was the first player to win premierships at three clubs and has also had one of the loudest voices in the growth and direction of the competition.

"In a little while we'll look back and realise how significant this time was and the inception of the NRLW," Elliott said.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

"When the competition came in, let's be honest no-one really cared. I'm not sugarcoating it.

"But the fact we're sitting here in a press conference room, we've got State of Origin where we have millions of people tune in.

"We go to a footy game and people know who we are; that's just crazy."

Elliott won two premierships at Brisbane in 2019 and 2020, before taking a title at Newcastle in 2022 and another at the Roosters in 2024.

The Tri-colours are unbeaten this year, headed into the finals with their only defeat in the past two seasons coming in the 2025 decider against Brisbane.

She was the Roosters' captain for their premiership in 2021 and has set the culture for the club, now a powerhouse of the competition.

In a career halted at times by pregnancy and injury, the mother of three played her first of seven Tests for Australia in 2016 and also played in seven Origins for NSW.

"The Roosters are going to be strong for a very long time because of that foundation that we've built and I'm proud of that," she said.

"What I love is seeing the ones in our systems really thriving from playing football from a young age and coming through and playing with us now."

AAP

title: Darwin homeless shelter residents to be moved 100km south to Batchelor
text:
Up to 150 people in transitional accommodation in Darwin will be relocated 100 kilometres south to the regional town of Batchelor when the Batten Road homeless shelter in Marrara closes next month.

Northern Territory Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill today announced the new facility would be stood up alongside emergency evacuation accommodation by October 11.

Ms Cahill said the decision to relocate the residents had come after negotiations with the owner of the YiSSA site in Darwin, Ausco , stalled amid a failed $3.5 million Commonwealth intervention.

Speaking to the media in Batchelor this morning, Ms Cahill said a number of options had been explored but the site was "the best option" that was available before AusCo's lease ended.

Robyn Cahill says many of the 230 adults and 150 children who had been living at the YiSSA facility have already been transitioned out. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Cahill said the government had been working to transition as many of the roughly 380 people who had been staying at YiSSA into alternative accommodation ahead of the move.

"There are a number of other people who have been on the housing list for quite some time but the work hadn’t been done to progress that," she said.

"We’ve been able to actually get people on the housing list, into appropriate housing accommodation, we’ve got around 30 people who we’ve relocated back to their [traditional] country, which is fantastic.

"We’ve got support from other community service providers who have a better arrangement for some of the people who need additional support in that facility and the we are left with around about 100 people that we’re still working with to see what their long-term prospect will be.

"So for those people, they’ll be able to come to the new facility and we’ll continue to work with them to find their long-term permanent accommodation solution."

Concern over access to services

Rose Laynbalaynba said she had been living at the Darwin shelter with her children for about two-and-a-half years while working as a language and culture lecturer at Charles Darwin University.

The new facility will sit alongside an up evacuation centre that was stood up for residents affected by devastating flooding in the region earlier this year. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Ms Laynbalaynba said the move was "going to be very hard".

"Batchelor is too far for these residents staying at YiSSA," she said.

"We have renal patients, how the hell do they come for their treatment if it’s that far?

"We need appointments to see the Centrelink, some of us have a job that is part time work.

" We need help and support, this is going from bad to bloody worse. "

Hundreds face homelessness as accommodation set to close Hundreds of residents fear they could be left homeless after the Northern Territory government announced it will shut a Darwin short-stay accommodation centre in less than 90 days.

But Ms Cahill said the Darwin facility was never intended to house people who were medically vulnerable and anyone requiring dialysis would "have accommodation provided to them close to where they get those services".

"We have been working very closely with the Department of Health to understand why people who weren’t necessarily the people who Batten Road was intended to assist were accommodated there and we’ve basically discovered that the Health Department weren’t made aware that those people needed that assistance," she said.

"These people are assessed for their suitability, they know what is required of them and anyone who needs to be close to medical services will be managed through the normal patient travel and Department of Health services system."

title: Key SA wave buoy to be redeployed a third time after lightning damage
text:
South Australia's long-suffering wave buoy is expected to be redeployed this week following a "lightning strike" in autumn that caused another lengthy outage.

The Bureau of Meteorology's (BOM) wave buoy off Cape du Couedic on Kangaroo island has suffered three outages since August 2024, including one that went for nine months.

It has only been functional for about 10 months in two years.

It most recently stopped transmitting data nearly four months ago on May 30 during stormy weather.

"Investigation of the damaged wave buoy showed severe electrical damage consistent with a lightning strike," a BOM spokesperson said.

"There are significant weather extremes where the Cape du Couedic wave buoy is located which can impact the equipment itself, but also the safety of retrieval and maintenance operations."

BOM says a lightning strike likely damaged the wave buoy, which had only just been repaired. (Supplied: Dave Newton)

Its troubles began in mid-2024 when the buoy started transmitting erroneous data and was taken offline in September.

The spokesperson said the bureau faced "global shortages for specialist replacement equipment [the mooring], causing delays for the Cape du Couedic wave buoy to return to service".

It took nine months to fix the buoy.

Then about five months later in November 2025 a mooring failure caused it to break free and wash up on Kangaroo Island, putting it out of commission for another six weeks.

The BOM spokesperson said the current issue was different and the bureau had "prioritised retrieving, assessing and reinstating the wave buoy, subject to weather conditions and safety requirements".

'Lives in danger' as SA wave buoy fails yet again The wave buoy off Kangaroo Island is the only such device operated by the Bureau of Meteorology in South Australia and is relied upon by professional divers.

"Return to service was dependent on the cause of the outage and available parts once the buoy was recovered," they said.

"Replacement parts have been procured. Repairs and redeployment is planned for this week, pending an appropriate period of safe weather conditions."

A critical weather station

When functioning, the wave buoy issues real time and historical data about significant and maximum wave heights, average and peak wave period, and swell direction.

Its data is used by commercial fishers, considered critical by the likes of abalone divers, as well as recreational fishers, divers and surfers.

It is the only wave buoy operated by BOM in SA and fishers and divers have been increasingly frustrated by the outages.

The ABC has asked the bureau how much money has been spent on repairs to the buoy since August 2024, but costs have not been divulged.

The buoy is considered critical by professional abalone divers. (Instagram: Polaccopaul)

"The bureau spent $96.5 million on a website which did not meet the needs of Australians while basic weather infrastructure has been allowed to fail," said federal opposition spokesperson for the environment David Nouri.

"This goes to priorities and competence. The bureau is already facing an independent review after the website debacle, while the auditor-general has found it was only partly effective at managing the assets in its observing network.

"South Australians are entitled to know how much has been spent trying to repair this buoy and why a permanent solution has not been delivered.

"Environment Minister Murray Watt should be demanding the bureau get the basics right."

The office of federal Environment Minister Murray Watt has been contacted several times during the outages but has directed inquiries back to the bureau.

title: ACT government minister censured over library opening hours
text:
City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne has become the third Labor minister to be censured by the ACT Legislative Assembly in less than a year.

The Canberra Liberals brought the censure motion against Ms Cheyne over weekend library closures and a bungle that cast doubt over thousands of seatbelt fines.

The seatbelt element was amended out of the motion, with the assembly instead passing the censure based on library opening hours 13 votes to 10.

Opposition leader Mark Parton said Ms Cheyne had "ignored" a motion passed by the assembly in June, which called on the government to pause a move to close public libraries on Sundays.

"Censure is the strongest tool this parliament has short of no confidence," Mr Parton said.

'I will not accept that candour is misconduct'

The motion was supported by the Liberals, the Greens and independent Fiona Carrick.

An emotional Ms Cheyne defended her track record, and expressed dismay about the premise of the motion, pointing out she had explained the "operational constraints" libraries were under.

"I do not and I will not accept that candour is misconduct and I certainly will not accept that it is contempt," Ms Cheyne said.

Canberra's libraries have been the subject of debate in the Assembly over staffing issues and unplanned closures. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She used her assembly speech to say options were being considered to reintroduce weekend hours at some libraries next year.

"That will include prioritising weekend branch access at Kippax and Erindale from July 2027," she said.

Ms Cheyne later issued a statement saying the government would "continue to improve and modernise library services across Canberra" and an evaluation of library operating arrangements would be published by March 2027.

Deputy Chief Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said it was "extraordinary" a minister was being censured for "doing their job".

A censure motion is a severe reprimand but is largely symbolic and carries no ongoing consequences aside from reputational damage.

'An electoral dead-end'

Leanne Castley gave a fiery speech criticising the censure motion. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

The censure debate became fiery at some points, with Liberal-turned-independent MLA Leanne Castley slamming her former party.

"We know that the opposition clearly intends to censure, smear and whinge their way to the 2028 election," she told the assembly.

"They are attracted to the excitement of censures and smears, but it is an electoral dead-end, even at the best of times."

Independent Thomas Emerson attempted to have the censure motion downgraded. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Fellow independent Thomas Emerson unsuccessfully attempted to downgrade the censure to an admonishment.

"We have other mechanisms to debate and condemn government decisions in the assembly, while reserving censure motions for clear instances of government incompetence," Mr Emerson said.

" If we lower the threshold and start using censure motions for every disagreement, they risk becoming meaningless. "

Ms Cheyne is the third minister this term to be censured by the assembly, following the censures of Yvette Berry and Chris Steel.

Before this term, the last time the ACT Legislative Assembly had censured an MLA was in 2011.

title: Melbourne council rejects bid to build new church in green wedge
text:
A new church proposed for protected land in Melbourne's outer south-east is unlikely to go ahead, after councillors knocked back an application for a planning permit.

The Bethel New Life Christian Fellowship had wanted to build the $3.5 million dollar church in a green wedge zone in Cranbourne South.

The green wedge was established to protect biodiversity, agricultural land and rural townships against development.

Despite council officers recommending the project proceed, the councillors rejected the application at a City of Casey council meeting on Tuesday night.

"Green wedges have a clear purpose," councillor Dave Perry told the meeting.

"They're meant to provide a physical buffer to urban sprawl."

The church group wanted to build its new place of worship along Cranbourne-Frankston Road. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The proposed development would have included a two-storey church for up to 400 patrons and 120 car parking spaces, built opposite a bustling residential development.

The religious group said it had outgrown its space in an industrial part of Dandenong, which serviced hundreds of people in Tamil and English.

"For a growing community, it's not possible to stay where we are," pastor John De Britto said.

Mr De Britto said he was disappointed with the council's decision.

"90 per cent of the church community live in Casey, so the council is not listening to those members of the community."

The Bethel New Life Christian Fellowship says it has outgrown its church in Dandenong. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The church group bought the $1.8 million site on Cranbourne-Frankston Road in the hopes that they would be able to continue servicing the congregation in a new home.

However, the application sparked controversy among the local community, with many raising concerns about its potential impact on biodiversity and traffic.

Despite more than 230 objections to the proposal, council officers had recommended approval subject to 56 conditions.

Cr Perry said the size of the building was central to the decision to reject the application.

"We're talking about a 3,515 square metre building that's up to nine metres high," he said.

The application to relocate the church group to a green wedge zone sparked controversy across the community. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

When a council refuses to grant a planning permit, the application can be appealed to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT).

Mr De Britto said the church's congregation would meet on Sunday to decide what to do next.

title: Third appeal lodged against Australian-record $150m native title payout
text:
Australia's largest ever native title payout will face appeals from three sides, with mining billionaire Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest's Fortescue becoming the latest group to challenge the landmark legal judgement.

In May, the Federal Court ordered the West Australian resources giant pay a record $150.3 million to a group of traditional owners for building four iron-ore mines in WA's north without their permission.

Late last month, the Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation (YNAC) and WA government lodged opposite appeals to each other in quick succession.

A spokesperson for Fortescue said it was forced to respond to the two appeals to protect its own legal position.

"Our cross-appeal restates positions we put forward at trial and seeks clarity on aspects of the judgement that we believe are inconsistent with existing legal principles and precedent," they said.

Fortescue's Solomon mine hub in the middle of WA's Pilbara region. (AAP: Will Russell)

The spokesperson said despite the court's judgement and the company's immediate payment, it did not bring the matter to an end.

"Fortescue has always wanted to resolve this long-running dispute," they said.

"We paid the full compensation award within 24 hours because we wanted the money to reach the Yindjibarndi community as quickly as possible."

Court found Fortescue liable

Fortescue's Solomon Hub sits on about 135 square kilometres of Yindjibarndi exclusive native title land and has produced estimated revenue of $80 billion since 2013.

Traditional owners not yet ready to end dispute with Forrest's Fortescue More than a fortnight after winning the largest native title compensation payout ever in Australia, a Yindjibarndi man returns to his country.

Contributions by the flagship operation have helped company chair Andrew Forrest's personal wealth surpass $33 billion.

Justice Stephen Burley found Fortescue had destroyed at least 124 spiritually significant sites in digging the mines, and permanently altered the landscape with its water extraction.

He said the miner was liable for $150 million for cultural losses affecting the Yindjibarndi people and another $150,000 in economic losses, plus compound interest.

When YNAC announced its appeal in August, chief executive Michael Woodley said lawyers for the native title body would target both branches of Justice Burley's verdict.

Michael Woodley says YNAC's appeal will target both the cultural loses and economic losses rulings. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

It followed a unanimous vote in Roebourne, more than 1,500 kilometres north-east of Perth, where many of the Yindjibarndi community's 500 or so members live.

A successful appeal could push the compensation figure closer to the $1.8 billion YNAC had initially claimed, applying what it described as an industry-standard royalty rate.

YNAC will also renew its argument that Fortescue systematically divided the Yindjibarndi people by funding a breakaway native title group and harmed their ability to practice traditional ceremonies.

'Manifestly excessive'

Documents filed to the Federal Court reveal the WA government's appeal follows similar grounds to its original case.

It disputed nearly every dimension of Justice Burley's judgement and labelled the compensation for cultural loss "manifestly excessive."

The State Solicitor's office wrote the Justice had failed to provide adequate reasons for a sum that was nearly three times greater than the amount awarded to the Northern Territory's Guradnji, Yanyuwa, and Yanyuwa-Marra people in February.

Tony Buti says the government's appeal is seeking clarity, while court filings slam the payout as "excessive". (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

At the time, WA Attorney-General Tony Buti said the appeal sought "clarity on the law", although one critic accused the government of attempting to appear "business friendly".

The state has previously suggested that compensation should be capped at $10 million, while Fortescue put the number at $8.1 million.

A court date has not yet been set.

title: Website crashes due to demand for Spirit of Tasmania bookings
text:
The Spirit of Tasmania website has crashed this morning as highly-anticipated tickets for the new Spirits IV and V were released for sale.

Tickets were set to go live at 10am but a notice on the website said it was experiencing high demand for bookings and users had been placed in a queue.

There was high demand as soon as the tickets went on sale. (www.spiritoftasmania.com.au)

At 11am, bookings were able to be viewed but not completed, causing an error message to pop up.

An error message appeared before customers could complete their bookings. (www.spiritoftasmania.com.au)

The booking site would not load for some customers. (www.spiritoftasmania.com.au)

Before today, tickets were only sold to the capacity of the previous Spirit vessels, and bookings were only available up to June 6, 2027.

With many sailing dates booked up until the end of the year, today's release included increased capacity on sold-out sailings, cheap fares and the first tickets for the new pet-friendly cabins.

The new Spirits will have increased capacity for caravans. (www.spiritoftasmania.com.au)

A key gateway to Tasmania

Spirits IV and V are set to start sailing the Bass Strait from October 31 after a years-long saga to replace the aging Spirits I and II, which have been sailing between Victoria and Tasmania since 2002.

Bungled ferry replacement project cost $717m more than forecast The Spirit of Tasmania ferry replacement program has cost $717 million more than was forecast in the original business case, a parliamentary inquiry has heard.

Delays and cost blowouts have plagued the rollout of the new ferries.

These included an $81 million bailout to a Finnish shipbuilder, and revelations that a new wharf in Devonport had ballooned in cost.

Operator TT-Line says the new ships will feature 301 cabins, carry an additional 470 passengers, and have three times the capacity for caravans.

Yesterday, TT-Line chief executive Chris Carbone described it as a new era.

"[It] marks an exciting milestone as we open bookings for Spirit of Tasmania IV and Spirit of Tasmania V and prepare to welcome passengers aboard for the very first time," he said.

A new Spirit of Tasmania ship passes one of the older, smaller ferries. (Supplied: TT-Line)

Government minister Jo Palmer said she was delighted to see such high demand.

"Isn't it just wonderful to hear that the incredible interest that has been shown now we are open and able to be taking tickets for the Spirit of Tasmania with the new ships?" she said.

"In regard to how the system is holding up, I'm sure there are a lot of people frantically working on that right now, but we are so excited at the level of interest that has come to our new Spirits."

" I don't think anyone can dampen our spirits today. "

TT-Line has been contacted for comment.

Visitors frustrated with system

Mornington Peninsula resident Jen Graham has been refreshing the website since 10am and finally secured tickets at 1pm.

She said she had been keenly awaiting the new allocation to help get her son and his car to university in Launceston.

"For a company that so heavily promoted and advertised this process, how on earth were they not prepared for the influx of bookings?" she asked.

Central Highlands resident Yvette Baker was unable to book tickets.

"I've travelled with the Spirit for over 10 years now and it's always been great," she said.

"It's just frustrating to plan for Christmas time as there aren't many bookings."

A resident who did not want to be named from Prospect Vale in Launceston was able to book tickets for her and her partner, car and caravan in June next year after waiting for the date to become available.

"It was an awful experience," they said. "It's been very, very stressful.

"So many people are stressed about Christmas and their pets. I'm very relieved."

title: Renshaw reveals secret behind milestone ODI century
text:
Matt Renshaw admits he may not have posted his first ODI century had he opened the batting for Australia against Zimbabwe.

Batting at six, Renshaw starred for the tourists in Harare, making 109 off 94 deliveries, as Australia recorded a 59-run win in the first of three ODIs.

The ODI ton was his first for Australia across any format since his only Test century in 2017, when he opened the batting against Pakistan at the SCG.

He recently returned to the Test arena, after a three-year absence, and again opened the batting in Australia's innings victory over Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Aussies defeat Zimbabwe Matt Renshaw plays a starring role with the bat, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

But he played down the batting order in his nine ODI matches prior to Harare.

Renshaw said avoiding the pressure of opening the batting helped him score his century.

"Higher up the order I [get] a bit giddy,'' Renshaw said.

"For me, my tempo when I come in the middle overs is just trying to hit the gaps, hit where the fielders aren't.

"With spin being a very big factor in that middle period … I see it as my strength. I really understood my role. It made it really simple for me."

Renshaw was named in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming series against South Africa.

Australia will face the Proteas in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

The next ODI against Zimbabwe will be played on Friday in Harare.

ABC/AAP

title: Ed Sheeran's support acts quit US tour after Macklemore dropped
text:
Four supporting acts on Ed Sheeran's US tour have abruptly quit in solidarity with rapper Macklemore, who has been dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.

Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, Danish band Lukas Graham, and US artist Finneas posted on Instagram that they were pulling out.

Rowe and Lukas Graham would have been replacements for Macklemore on Sheeran's remaining US dates, while Sheeran's touring band, Beoga, had been performing several songs — including some the Irish folk band co-wrote — with Sheeran around the middle of each set.

Finneas is one of the acts to announce they are pulling out of The Loop tour. (AP: Jordan Strauss/Invision, File)

Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said on Instagram.

"I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."

Pressure mounts on Sheeran

The moves by his fellow artists put enormous pressure on Sheeran, who has tried to avoid politics and taking a side in the Gaza conflict, arguing that his fans do not come to his shows to hear politics.

Rowe and Beoga each cited their country's history in their statements explaining their decisions.

"We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be," Beoga said.

Aaron Rowe has pulled out of the tour, citing his support for Palestinians. (AP: Scott A Garfitt/Invision, File)

Rowe called Sheeran a friend and said the British singer-songwriter changed his life.

"But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," he said, adding that he could not "stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up".

Loading...

Meanwhile, Lukas Graham, the band that had hits with Mama Said and 7 Years, expressed gratitude to Sheeran and called it "a difficult decision".

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," the band posted, seemingly referring to billionaire Robert Kraft's role in Macklemore's removal from the tour.

Emails seeking comment were sent to Sheeran and the tour's promoter, the Messina Touring Group.

Crisis started with Macklemore being dropped

Sheeran weighed in on Macklemore's removal after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments onstage during their tour, saying the promoters made the decision.

The British singer also said he refused to be drawn into a public discussion about the war in Gaza.

Macklemore dropped from Sheeran tour Macklemore says he has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour over pro-Palestinian comments made on stage earlier this month.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran wrote on Instagram on Tuesday, local time.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

Sheeran's statement came a day after Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after saying "Free Palestine" while introducing his protest song Hind's Hall at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium earlier this month.

"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it is in no way criticism of you," he said during the concert.

Macklemore said on Instagram on Monday that New England Patriots owner and billionaire Mr Kraft had rallied support among some stadium owners and told Sheeran they would not allow him to perform at their venues if Macklemore stayed on the tour.

In a statement on Monday, Mr Kraft said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community".

Macklemore denies being antisemitic and says conflating antisemitism with criticism of Israel's actions aims to avoid Israeli accountability.

Mr Kraft's representatives did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about the other musical artists' actions.

Sheeran says 'I am not complicit'

A growing chorus of organisations and experts say Israel's wartime actions in Gaza amount to genocide — an accusation Israel vehemently rejects.

Macklemore was scheduled to perform at eight of the 10 shows Sheeran has remaining on his stadium tour, which is scheduled to resume in Philadelphia on Saturday. Ahead are stops at Gillette Stadium, Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium and Indianapolis's Lucas Oil Stadium.

In his social media post, Sheeran said he "spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge", but that "the venue's and promoter's decision was final".

He wrote that he tried to use his music to "bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together" and that while he had personal views about "this devastating conflict", he chose not to speak publicly because people who came to his shows "do not expect a political forum".

"I am not complicit. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes," Sheeran said.

" However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace. I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. "

AP/Reuters

title: AI firm's ASX listing may be second-largest behind Telstra
text:
AI data centre developer Firmus Technologies is courting investors in Asia and Australia ahead of a widely expected multi-billion-dollar share market float next month.

The company has been making headlines over its expansions and resulting community concerns, as well as through its partnerships.

Last week Firmus announced it had signed a multi-year deal with OpenAI for two new AI factory sites in Malaysia.

Firmus's AI factory in Singapore, which uses the company's technology to submerge its data clusters. (Supplied: Firmus)

At the same time, the company has been growing its presence in northern Tasmania with three data centre projects and a flurry of sports sponsorships, including with the Tasmania Devils AFL team.

One AI data centre is currently under construction in Launceston, where its parent company is headquartered, and another near George Town has council approval while a site at Wesley Vale is still awaiting approval.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff is shown around Firmus's Launceston facility by Mr Rosenfield and Mr Curtis. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Plans are also underway for projects in South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, Western Australia and the ACT.

Firmus already has significant operations in Singapore, and over the next 24 months, it says it hopes to have seven AI data centres across four countries.

Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder. The AI company and club say it's a natural pairing — but not all are convinced.

This narrative of aggressive expansion will stoke interest in its expected float on the Australian share market next month.

Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in an initial public offering (IPO), which could value the company at more than $50 billion, depending on what proportion of the company is sold.

If that pans out, it could make Firmus the second-largest float in Australian history, after the federal government raised $14 billion by selling a third of Telstra three decades ago, valuing the entire company at $42 billion.

Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis have sought to allay public concerns about the amount of energy and water the data centres would require. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Based on its share price yesterday, Telstra had a market value of $53 billion.

An important caveat for many of the figures being touted in the financial press for Firmus's float is that they are based on conjecture and hype.

The company's public offer document, the prospectus that potential investors will review, has yet to be lodged with the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).

Firmus Technologies has plans for data centres across Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

The valuation reports are based partly on an invitation for a "roadshow" in Asian and Australian capitals sent out to potential investors by investment banks handling the float for Firmus.

The roadshow will help determine how much demand there is for stock, based on forecast earnings.

A spokesperson for Firmus declined to comment on the likely size of the capital raising, or how much of the company might be sold, which will depend on the demand.

'Mum and dad investors' also likely for IPO, expert says

Sam Baker, private wealth adviser at Shadforth Financial Group, told the ABC it was widely known Firmus had been looking to debut this year on the ASX.

"It now appears as if the company is fronting investors both in Asia, and soon to be Australia, as a preamble to looking to do an initial public offering of up to $7 billion," Mr Baker said.

"They're telling the story of the business, providing details, which will largely be provided in any prospectus for the initial public offering.

" But it's about sort of gauging interest as to what or whether investors would be interested and at what price they would be potentially prepared to pay for any shares in an initial public offering. "

The data centre under construction at St Leonards, Launceston. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Mr Baker said investors in Australia and overseas would likely be interested.

"In an initial public offering, they tend to have cornerstone or institutional investors, but I would expect a raising of this size will also be looking to attract retail, or mum and dad, investors," he said.

Mr Baker said while IPOs could be used for the founders to "cash out", it seemed Firmus was raising funds to support the rollout of its AI data centres across Australia and South-East Asia.

From Bitcoin to AI

Firmus's most advanced project is at St Leonards in Launceston, and it has approval for another at Long Reach, near George Town, in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone.

The company is seeking approval for another at Wesley Vale in Tasmania's north-west.

A visualisation of the Firmus AI data centre planned near George Town, in northern Tasmania. (Supplied)

Firmus has struggled to gain a social licence in Tasmania, but Mr Baker did not believe that would necessarily impact the IPO.

"Broader institutional investors are mainly focused on getting a return," he said.

" Whether or not there is some resistance across the retail shareholders, that will remain to be seen. "

Firmus began as a bitcoin miner in 2019, subsequently pivoting to data centre development.

Its co-CEO Oliver Curtis was sentenced to two years' jail in 2016 for conspiring to commit insider trading.

The trial heard how he shared in $1.4 million of illegal profits from insider trading using confidential information between May 2007 and June 2008.

Firmus co-CEO Oliver Curtis with his wife Roxy Jacenko. (Instagram: Roxyjacenko)

In October 2025, Mr Curtis was asked about his reflections on the ordeal and whether Tasmanians could trust Firmus.

"The experience of the past presents an opportunity for the future," he told ABC Radio Hobart at the time.

"It's all about resilience, it's all about how you get back on the horse, and it's all about basically making sure that you are completing what you believe you need to complete.

"For me, this is about more than an individual; this is about a company.

"I'm so fortunate we have a hugely amazing, talented team around us — and that's the story."

title: ‘It’s time to move on’: NRLW greats Elliott and Baxter call time on careers

SportNRLNRLW 2026 ‘It’s time to move on’: NRLW greats Elliott and Baxter call time on careers Billie Eder Updated September 16, 2026 — 2:27pm ,first published September 13, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. There are few people more influential in women’s rugby league than Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter, which is why it felt like the end of an era when the Roosters duo announced they’d both be retiring from the game at the end of 2026. The news, while unexpected, was unsurprising from Baxter who, at 32 years old, has already made a comeback to the game twice – the first after giving birth to her second son Beauden in 2022, and the second after she ruptured her ACL in 2024. Corban Baxter with her sons Carter and Beauden. James Brickwood “I probably struggled the last couple of years, returning from my ACL,” Baxter said. “I think my body’s started to slow down. I’ve tried to push through that probably the last couple of seasons, and then obviously having a young family, it’s a lot of time away from them, and I’ve been doing it for the whole life of my 15-year-old son [Carter].

Advertisement

“It was a bit of a family decision too, to make sure that I can have more time with them, but it was something that wasn’t solidified until probably earlier on in this season.” Elliott’s announcement came as much more of a shock. The 28-year-old made her return to the game this year after having her first child Gigi, and went straight into the NSW Blues Origin side that won the series 3-0. Millie Elliott with her husband Adam, their daughter Gigi and his son Lenny. James Brickwood As Roosters coach John Strange said on Wednesday, both Baxter and Elliott are at the top of their game and remain pivotal parts of his undefeated Tricolours team that is eyeing a third grand final appearance in three years. “I just knew that it was time for me,” Elliott said. “I’ve always played because I love the game. And, you know, women’s rugby league players that are playing right now are playing because they genuinely love the game and I still really love the game.

Advertisement

“I’ve only just thought about this in the last six to eight weeks, and that’s something that I’ve had to process with and chat to the girls with. It’s never been something that I’ve thought of before, and I feel really content with what I’ve achieved in rugby league. “Having my daughter Gigi and being able to bring her along the ride this year has been very special, but it’s time to move on for that next chapter of my career and life ... I just knew myself that I was ready.” Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter announce their retirement from rugby league. James Brickwood The term trailblazer is one that gets thrown around too often in rugby league, but for these two women the title certainly rings true. They’ve been there from the start. Elliott became the first NRLW player to win four premierships when she lifted the trophy with the Tricolours in 2024, after previously doing it with Newcastle in 2022 and Brisbane in 2019 and 2020. She’s also won the Origin shield four times with NSW.

Advertisement

Baxter was the first Roosters captain to lift the NRLW premiership trophy for the club in 2021, and she was in the NSW team that won four Origin titles between 2016 and 2019. Both have been pioneers of the women’s game, which has grown from a four-round competition in 2018 to 12 teams in 2026, and now includes a reserve-grade competition that runs alongside the NRLW season. Roosters captain Corban Baxter poses with the Premiership trophy after her team’s victory over the Dragons in the 2021 NRLW grand final. Getty Images “When the competition came in, let’s be honest, no one really cared – I’m not sugarcoating it,” Elliott said. “The comp was very small, I guess a little bit, I don’t want to say tokenistic, but we played each other once, and there were four teams. It was a very short comp.

Advertisement

“But the fact we’re sitting here in a press conference room, we’ve got State of Origin where we have thousands [attend], millions of people tune in to watch it on television in prime-time slots... “The fact that we go to a footy game, and people know who we are, that’s just crazy. I really want to give credit to the people in rugby league who profile the women’s game. It’s changed our lives, and it’s crazy to think what it’s going to do for this next generation of players coming through. ” Both retiring stars are calling time on rugby league to focus on their family and the next chapter in their careers. Both already have roles in the media – Elliott with Nine, the publisher of this masthead, while Baxter appears on Fox’s NRLW coverage and also does some coaching. To bow out with one more premiership for the Roosters would be the cherry on top.

Advertisement

“We would love to finish on a high and get that premiership with the girls,” Baxter said. “Retiring or not, that’s the goal. We want to win premierships, and we’ve done our reflections on last year, the fire is well and truly burning within, as a team. “To go out on a high would be a dream come true.” ‘They can be beaten’: Undefeated Roosters aren’t a sure thing for title, says V’landys As the NRLW finals get under way this week, the 2026 premiership appears to be a two-horse race between the Roosters and the Titans.

Advertisement

The Roosters are undefeated this season and have a week off before the preliminary finals next weekend, while the Titans, who also have a week off, have only lost once this year – their round one match against the Tricolours. Roosters NRLW captain Isabelle Kelly is ready for another finals campaign. Oscar Colman It sets up a potentially mouth-watering decider, with last year’s premiers Brisbane the only team seemingly capable of stopping the top two. ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys conceded the Roosters’ dominance may not be good for the women’s competition – they have only lost three games in the past three years, and their most recent defeat was to Brisbane in the 2025 grand final – but he is confident teams are capable of stepping up to end their streak. “Look, it isn’t [a good thing], but the thing is that they can be beaten,” V’landys said.

Advertisement

“As I’ve learnt in the racing industry, a favourite can be beaten, and I think there are a few more teams there that will give the Roosters an absolute run for their money. “So, I don’t think it’s going to be as dominant as what the season’s been – the semi-finals go to another level.” The Tricolours go into their week off fit and healthy, a welcome change from last year when halfback Tarryn Aiken damaged her ACL just before the finals. The Roosters have been unstoppable in 2026. Getty Images The pain of last year’s grand final, which the Broncos won via a 65th minute try to Mele Hufanga, is still fresh in the mind of Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly. And while the team is undefeated in 2026 – something Kelly is adamant they have not spoken about – she is under no illusions that they will cruise through the finals to claim the premiership.

Advertisement

“Finals footy is a different breed,” Kelly said. “I think you can go all the way through, build consistency, be undefeated, but then we’ve obviously bowed out twice in a semi-final and then had that heartbreak of losing a grand final. “It’s finals footy, everyone steps up, the game goes to a new level. I think we’ve seen it in the NRL this week with the games just played, and some of those games were insane.” The Titans have been responsible for some Roosters heartbreak in the past. Gold Coast won a gritty semi-final 12-0 in 2023, but lost to Newcastle in the grand final. The Gold Coast are certainly capable of causing an upset again this year. “They’ve been so good; they’ve been unreal,” Kelly said of the Titans.

Advertisement

“I think they’re one of the hot contenders, to be honest, to be in that grand final, and I think they deserve to have the week off, same as us, because of the form they’ve been in.” Titans captain Georgia Hale and Roosters counterpart Isabelle Kelly. Oscar Colman Titans captain Georgia Hale – who was part of the team that lost that 2023 grand final – has total belief in her team. Not only are they battle-hardened, she said, after defeating every other finals team in the regular season – Broncos, Tigers, Knights and Raiders – but they are also capable of turning the tables on the Roosters in the decider. “Absolutely [we can beat them]. The belief is there, and gosh, that would be such a good feeling,” Hale said.

Advertisement

“To be the best, you want to beat the best. So yeah, just say when and where.” After 15 years, the Tigers are playing in the finals again It’s been 15 long years, but the Wests Tigers are finally playing finals football again. For the first time since 2011, a top-grade Tigers team will play a match at the business end of the season, thanks to the club’s NRLW side sealing a top-four finish with a 7-4 record during the 11-match regular season. Wests Tigers captain Kezie Apps has been with the team since their inaugural year in 2022. George Chan

Advertisement

It’s an impressive turnaround for a team that finished with just one win, and the wooden spoon for the second year in a row in 2025. The last Wests Tigers team to play finals was Tim Sheens’ 2011 squad that included Benji Marshall, Lote Tuqiri and Robbie Farah. One of the most significant changes for the NRLW team this year has been the arrival of coach Craig Sandercock. “If you were to say to me at the start of the year, you’re playing finals footy, I would have 100 per cent taken that,” Sandercock said. “It’s been a great, great year, and you could probably consider it a really successful year from the club, especially with where we’ve come from.”

Advertisement

The team always had potential, said Sandercock, but there were a handful of areas that required improvement. “When I watched all their games from last year, they only won one game, but there were periods in every game that they competed, and they competed hard, and it was just, I suppose, some key moments last year that really cost them,” Sandercock said. “Then that fed into that mindset of, here we go again, and then they concede another try and another try. So, for us, it was all about trying to build some resilience and really work hard on icing or winning those key moments in games that can lead to positive results.” Wests Tigers NRLW coach Craig Sandercock. NRL Images The recruitment of veteran players Raecene McGregor and Shaylee Bent has also been a huge boost, and those experienced players have joined forces with captain Kezie Apps and forward Sarah Togatuki – who have been with the club since that first 2023 season – to steer the team into the finals.

Advertisement

“I feel like this year the coach and the recruitment [team] have done a great job of finding that balance [between youth an experience],” said Apps. “We’ve still got our young girls coming through who are learning and who are going really good, but we’ve also got that great balance of the leaders and the experience within the group as well. Related Article NRL 2026 The Dolphins are one win from a grand final. They should thank Spencer Leniu “It’s obviously been a big change this year from going from only winning one game last year, and now here we are near finals, and we’ve come fourth. “Reflecting on the season that we’ve had ... and comparing that to last year coming last and then coming fourth, I think that’s something that needs to be celebrated and something that needs to be recognised of how hard the girls have worked to get to where we are.” The Tigers will play Canberra, who they lost 22-10 to in the final round of the season, in week one of the finals.

As the New Zealand Warriors attempt to keep their NRL season alive and avenge their qualifying final defeat to the Dolphins, one of the most enigmatic try-scorers in the club’s history will launch a new chapter in a rival code. David Fusitu’a has been quietly plying his trade in rugby union, far removed from the spotlight, having made the move to Brisbane, where he has spent two seasons with Brothers, winning the Hospital Cup premiership this year in the process. Now he has been called into the Queensland Reds’ fold for their forthcoming Super Rugby Australia clash with the New South Wales Waratahs. David Fusitu’a (pictured on the left in his Warriors days, and on the right with the Reds) will make his comeback to top-flight sport with the Queensland Reds this weekend. Getty/Reds Media The 31-year-old 106-kilogram flyer played 106 games for the Warriors – scoring 61 tries, many with some freakish, air-defying finishes – before departing for the English Super League for three years with Leeds Rhinos. He also managed nine Test caps for Tonga and two for New Zealand.

Advertisement

Fusitu’a admits that when he drew the curtain on his England venture, he felt he still had something to offer on the field. Eager to give the 15-man game a try, he consulted a friend in New Zealand, who linked him up with Brothers. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow But while a comeback to professional football full-time was not on his radar for now, Fusitu’a was quick to answer a “surprise” SOS from new Reds coach Vern Cotter, and will line up at outside-centre for his new side at the Santos Festival of Rugby in Roma this weekend. “It’s been a crazy couple of years,” Fusitu’a said. “I finished up in England with Leeds Rhinos and moved back to this side of the world. I knew I wanted to give rugby a crack, and just by chance, I ended up here in Brisbane. “It’s obviously a weird time when you’re adjusting to life after professional rugby, and I would always think to myself during rugby, ‘Is there something else I’m passionate about outside rugby?’

“I’ve found it in youth work lately, and have enjoyed giving back to kids in need, but also spending a bit more time with the family and being able to give back to them.” Fusitu’a will be joined in the Reds’ squad by former Wallabies flyer Sefa Naivalu, as Cotter ushers in reinforcements to cover injuries to Izaia Perese (calf), Josh Flook (torn achilles), and Lachie Anderson (facial fracture) in the aftermath of the club’s 29-28 defeat to the Western Force. Loading But even with a new challenge ahead of him, Fusitu’a could not resist looking towards what awaits his old Warriors teammates on Sunday night, when they square off in an elimination semi-final against Newcastle at Eden Park. New Zealand had the chance to lock in a preliminary final last weekend, after they led 16-8 deep into the second half, only to succumb to a Herbie Farnworth-inspired Dolphins comeback.

His fab five can right those wrongs “It definitely wasn’t the result I’m sure the boys were wanting, and us fans, but they get another chance. I’m a big Warriors supporter, I obviously played there and am still a big supporter of the boys and have a good few mates who are running around there,” Fusitu’a said. “Players like Chanel Harris-Tavita are still running around. He was still quite young at the time when I was there, but he’s come through the system, and it’ll be very special for him. “They’ve still got to get the job done, but I have big belief in that squad and what they’re building.” The Reds’ looming match will be the first time this year five-eighth Tom Lynagh will play back-to-back games, after a hamstring issue and illness limited him to barely 18 minutes of Super Rugby in 2026.

Collingwood champion Scott Pendlebury’s move to the Gold Coast as a free agent is likely to dilute the compensation the Suns would receive for losing Ben King, complicating the coveted spearhead’s planned move to Hawthorn. The Suns and Hawks were stunned to discover that if the AFL’s games record holder and oldest player moved as a free agent to the Gold Coast that it would potentially impact the compensation the club would receive for losing King. Scott Pendlebury of the Magpies and Massimo D’Ambrosio of the Hawks contest the ball. Getty Images It had been assumed that at Pendlebury’s age - he turns 39 in January - his move would not draw compensation for Collingwood, nor effect compensation for the Suns if King left as a free agent. King is yet to formally declare Hawthorn as his preferred destination but has told the Suns he wants to leave as a free agent to return to Victoria.

Advertisement

Hawthorn have been hoping that the Suns would not match contract terms for the restricted free agent and accept the expected compensation pick at selection seven in the draft. Pendlebury coming in as a free agent could push any King compensation back to an end of first round draft pick. Loading If there was a risk of the compensation for King being pushed back to an end of first round pick because of Pendlebury’s arrival, the Suns would be likely to match the contract terms and force Hawthorn into a trade for King. Having to trade for King would then impact the Hawk’s ability to trade for Zach Merrett from Essendon, who is expected to again ask for a trade to Hawthorn this year.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The ‘Butters rule’ the AFL should introduce to fix a shonky system Free agency compensation is determined based on the net result of free agents entering and leaving the club. Clubs are not formally told in advance what compensation pick they would receive from free agents coming in and out and the AFL formula for deciding compensation is deliberately kept confidential. The Pendlebury position is academic for now as no contract terms have been lodged with the AFL for either Pendlebury or King, in order for the league to officially decide on compensation, but the clubs have been warned that the veteran’s age is only one of three factors to consider in free agency. The amount and length of the contract is just as important. Above the age of 31, it doesn’t matter how old a player is as far as free agency compensation is concerned. To preserve their potential compensation for King, Pendlebury and the Suns could ask Collingwood to delist him. That way he could go to the Suns as a delisted free agent.

Delisted free agents do not draw compensation. Collingwood, however, have been reluctant to delist Pendlebury, being uncomfortable with the idea of delisting the club’s greatest ever player. Zach Merrett is likely to request a trade to Hawthorn again. Getty Images The Suns and Collingwood could also do a minor trade for the former captain and two time premiership player. Such an arrangement occurred when former Hawthorn premiership captain Sam Mitchell moved to West Coast at the end of his career. Like Pendlebury’s move to the Suns, it was part of a transition plan into coaching after a brief playing period.

Dabble, a social media-linked betting platform, has been slapped with more than $1 million in penalties after it breached self-exclusion laws, kept the accounts of more than 150 problem gamblers open and sent marketing material to them more than 800 times. The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) on Wednesday announced its investigation into the wagering platform – that allows users to copy bets from friends, former sports stars or other personalities – found a range of breaches of national self-exclusion laws known as BetStop. Dabble was fined more than $1 million for breaching self-exclusion laws. iStock The ACMA said Dabble, for which betting giant Tabcorp paid $33 million for a 20 per cent stake in 2022, failed to close 157 wagering accounts after the account holders registered with BetStop. The betting platform founded in 2020 and known for its sponsorship of the National Basketball League and Supercars Championship, also sent 165 self-excluded people a total of 839 electronic messages as either SMS, emails or app push notifications, the ACMA found.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Online gambling $6b betting giant had 500 problem-gambling breaches, but the regulator took too long to fine it BetStop was launched in 2023 as part of Australia’s self-exclusion laws aimed at allowing gamblers fearing or fighting addiction to have all of their accounts closed. Operators must also cease sending them marketing. Additionally, signing up to BetStop bans an individual from opening a new account with any platform licensed to operate in Australia. Wagering companies are obliged to inform customers about BetStop in any electronic messages promoting or advertising gambling. The ACMA also found Dabble sent 45 customers more than 2000 push notifications without including information about BetStop, in breach of the laws. Dabble, which is led by former PointsBet and CrownBet executive Tom Rundle as CEO, posted a $14.4 million profit in 2025. ACMA member Carolyn Lidgerwood said “these were serious breaches by Dabble” which had the potential to cause real harm.

Advertisement

“People who register with BetStop have made a clear decision to exclude themselves from online wagering,” she said. “Providers must respect that decision by closing their accounts promptly and ensuring they are not targeted with gambling promotions.” “BetStop is an important consumer protection measure, but it only works if wagering companies follow the rules,” Lidgerwood said. The $1.069 million in penalties Dabble has now paid were part of a two-year court-enforceable undertaking, requiring the company to conduct an independent review of its compliance systems and make the investment required to implement recommended improvements. “If Dabble breaches its undertaking, the ACMA can take the company to court to enforce terms,” the regulator said. When this masthead contacted Dabble’s publicly available email address for comment, its automated chatbot ROGER referred media inquiries to its public relations team. When asked for that email address, ROGER said: “We don’t have a publicly listed communications or public relations contact available for media inquiries.”

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Ladbrokes warns customers: gamble, or have accounts depleted ROGER said Dabble’s only published contact details were a physical mailing address for its headquarters based in Darwin. Gambling industry critics have suggested that companies are drawn to register in the Northern Territory due to favourable tax and regulations. After this story was first published, a Dabble spokesperson sent this masthead a statement which said the company “regret(s) that these contraventions occurred and take responsibility for instances where our internal BetStop controls did not perform as intended”. “Dabble confirms the ACMA’s investigation found no accounts were able to be accessed, and no bets were placed by Betstop registered customers. However, we recognise the overriding importance of meeting our responsible gambling and regulatory obligations and have strengthened our controls to reduce the risk of this occurring again,” the spokesperson said. The ACMA has previously come under fire for taking so long to conduct its investigations that it missed the 12-month window in which it could issue a penalty. Changes coming into effect next year extend the window to 24 months, and increase the maximum penalties for each breach of the rules. title: Barkly jags rich rare earths across 23km in NT
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Barkly jags rich rare earths across 23km in NT Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 16, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In what can only be described as a stellar assay-results debut, Barkly Rare Earths has hit significant rare earths mineralisation in every one of the first 28 holes assayed from a maiden drilling campaign at its flagship Barkly project in the Northern Territory. Results from the company’s 10,000-metre phase one resource expansion program have confirmed a massive, shallow, flat-lying mineralised system, with significant intercepts returned from holes drilled up to 23 kilometres apart, flagging the system’s huge potential size. A reverse circulation drill rig in action at Barkly Rare Earths’ maiden drilling campaign in the Northern Territory. The campaign is geared towards testing extensions to Barkly’s existing 40-million-tonne inferred mineral resource, which grades 2100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). Based on these first numbers, it appears to be well on its way. Intriguingly, the current resource is largely split between northern and southern deposits, leaving almost 15km of virtually untouched ground in between for the drill bit to put to the truth detector. That sizeable gap helps explain Barkly’s lofty exploration target of 200 million to one billion tonnes grading between 1600ppm and 1900ppm TREO. Highlights from the first batch of assays include a 2-metre hit grading 2716 ppm TREO from just 11m, featuring a higher-grade 0.5-metre core assaying an impressive 6064 ppm TREO. Another hole returned a 1.5-metre section grading 3228 ppm TREO from 15m, including a 0.5-metre interval at a solid 5170 ppm TREO.

Advertisement

‘Our ambition is to define a large-scale, high-grade resource.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Notably, the mineralisation is not only high-grade but also rich in the valuable magnet rare earth oxides (MREO), which currently make up 34 per cent of the company’s inferred mineral resource of TREO. The MREO include yttrium, neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, some of the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are essential for manufacturing high-strength permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. In a stunning outcome, MREO made up a consistently high 31 to 40 per cent of the TREO in 27 of the 28 fresh intercepts. The project itself is no run-of-the-mill sediment-hosted rare earths play, with mineralisation stretching through laterally extensive, near-horizontal Cretaceous sandstones and unusually tied to aluminium-phosphate-sulphate (APS) minerals. Adding to the project’s appeal, the mineralisation starts at shallow depths, from as little as 3m below surface in some areas, pointing towards the potential for a simple, low-cost open pit mining operation. Furthermore, the company says concentrations of the deleterious radioactive elements uranium and thorium are consistently low, a significant advantage for processing and a key feature that distinguishes it from many hard rock rare earth deposits.

Advertisement

Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “Twenty-eight holes assayed and twenty-eight intercepts — that is a very satisfying result, and the holes 23 km apart look like the same flat-lying horizon we mapped. Our ambition is to define a large-scale, high-grade resource, and results like these are why we are drilling another 300-plus holes.” The company recently announced a stunning 99 per cent extraction of high-value MREO from a single-stage metallurgical test on material from its namesake project. The result was achieved using a simple initial caustic conversion followed by a hydrochloric acid leach. Importantly, the test separated 92 per cent of the phosphorus impurities into the caustic solution, with no measurable rare earths detected, marking a significant technical win that could simplify and reduce the cost of downstream purification. Barkly only listed on the ASX in January this year following an oversubscribed $8 million IPO. The company is now furiously drilling to deliver an updated mineral resource estimate by the end of the year. The results come at a time when Western nations are scrambling to secure their own supplies of critical minerals and reduce their reliance on China. Beijing recently tightened its grip on the market by placing export controls on several key heavy rare earths, creating a perfect storm for explorers such as Barkly, as it chases what could emerge as a potentially globally significant deposit outside of China.

Advertisement

Barkly has drilled 68 holes to date, with assays from the first 28 now in. Samples from another 30 holes are currently at the laboratory, with a continuous flow of results expected through the final quarter of the year. The company plans to drill a further 300-plus holes to continue probing the extent of what appears to be a massive mineralised system. With a 100 per cent strike rate from the get-go, a mineralised footprint that already stretches for tens of kilometres and the all-important magnet metals showing up in spades, Barkly has certainly hit the ground running. With hundreds more drill holes planned and assays from dozens more already in the lab, the company should be providing plenty of news flow to keep the market interested. If these early numbers are a sign of things to come, Barkly’s Northern Territory story could get interesting very quickly. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting?
