title: The 31-year-old who might end up as the world’s most educated person
text:
Advertisement

BusinessEntrepreneurshipEducation The 31-year-old who might end up as the world’s most educated person Scott Cacciola September 16, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Early in the autumn semester of the 2025-26 academic year, Lisa Belkin, an adjunct professor at Columbia University’s journalism school, realised that one of her students, Jamie Beaton, had yet to show up for class. Belkin, who avoids combing the internet for information about her students, knew nothing about Beaton. She was curious about his absence, though, so she reached out to a dean, who sent an email. Jamie Beaton is hungry for degrees. NYT Beaton was apologetic in his reply, saying he had mixed up his schedule. He was in New Zealand, teaching a course in entrepreneurship at the University of Auckland, but would be back in New York the next week. That was when Belkin decided to break her rule. Who was this guy?

Advertisement

Beaton, she learned, had graduated magna cum laude from Harvard University in 2016, picking up a master’s degree in applied mathematics along the way. He had gone on to collect an MBA from Stanford University. Then a law degree from Yale University. That was followed by a doctor of philosophy in public policy from Oxford, where he was a Rhodes scholar – all before age 28. Related Article Medicine She lost her sight. Her Wall Street billionaire father bet on a daring new treatment Attending classes remotely and in person, he earned additional master’s degrees from – deep breath – the University of Pennsylvania (education entrepreneurship), Stanford (education technology), Princeton University (finance), Cornell University (healthcare policy and economics), Dartmouth College (implementation science), King’s College London (war studies) and Tsinghua University in Beijing (global affairs). Still, there was more: Beaton, who was born and raised in New Zealand, was a founder and the chief executive of Crimson Education, a college admissions counselling service that has been valued at more than $US600 million ($840 million). A week after his apologetic reply, Beaton made his first appearance in Belkin’s classroom. As the semester went on, he did not miss an assignment.

Advertisement

“He was a joy to get to know,” Belkin said. “But it was also the weirdest relationship I’ve ever had with a student.” ‘Passions and curiosities’ A 168-centimetres-tall personification of naked ambition whose LinkedIn profile has been the subject of memes and Reddit threads, Beaton has gone to the head of a rarefied class – perpetual students. In his final year of high school, Beaton took more than twice the number of required courses. He was admitted to 25 universities, including Harvard, Yale and Princeton. AP If he continues collecting advanced degrees at such a swift pace, he will surpass Benjamin B. Bolger, who has racked up 16 at age 50. He might even beat Michael Nicholson, an octogenarian forever scholar with more than 30 degrees to his name.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Billionaires Billionaire’s $6.3m ‘bride price’ stunt could backfire Away from his studies, Beaton, 31, has become a player in the field of college admissions counselling. His clients pay between $US30,000 and $US200,000 for a multiyear program designed to enhance their children’s chances of getting into top universities. His own academic background has raised some questions, starting with: How can this be real? Is it education as performance art? An elaborate marketing ploy for his business? The truth, Beaton said, is more prosaic. “The first five degrees had a clear skill acquisition component to them,” he said. “Since then, it’s really been about following different passions and curiosities.”

Advertisement

We met on a recent afternoon in Manhattan, not far from where he lives with his wife, Priscilla Beaton. His day was crowded with appointments, including an evening event at the Harvard Club in Midtown, where he and his Crimson Education colleagues would hold a meet-and-greet with potential clients. “I love the action, and I love a jam-packed day,” he said. “It’s good fun.” So many things are, according to Beaton, “good fun”. An abridged list: helping students decode the college admissions process. Studying the viability of distressed companies. Grabbing snacks in the Amtrak cafe car. Reading big books in one gulp. Riding the fastest roller coaster in the world on a recent trip to Saudi Arabia. He was cheerful and accommodating. He spoke rapidly, in fully formed paragraphs. Shortly before we met, he emailed me a 61-page legal notice stating that Crimson Education had initiated a $US28 million hostile takeover of Kip McGrath, an international tutoring provider. He keeps up with his studies even while travelling the world on business. A few weeks ago, he was in India when he submitted his end-of-semester project for a course at Brown University, where he is working toward a master’s in data science. He said he tries to get six hours of sleep a night.

Advertisement

“Oh, he’s lying,” John Key, a former prime minister of New Zealand, said in a telephone interview. Key, the chair of Crimson Education, considers Beaton the second-brightest New Zealander, behind the noted scientist Ernest Rutherford, who died nearly 90 years ago. “And I’m only saying that because it’s hard to take it away from the guy who split the atom,” Key said. Beaton has amassed quite a collection of college T-shirts. NYT Amy Chua, the author of Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother, a 2011 memoir about her hard-driving parenting style, was one of Beaton’s professors at Yale Law School. In recent years she has written more letters of recommendation for him than she can count.

Advertisement

“He can’t stop applying to things,” she said. She acknowledged that his story sounds apocryphal. “Jamie is so unusual that I wouldn’t have been surprised if someone had said to me, ‘Oh, he invented the whole thing – he doesn’t even have a mother’,” Chua said. ‘I want to work’ The making of the boy who wanted to know everything began in Auckland, New Zealand, where he was the only child of a single mother, Paula Beaton. She was pregnant when she and Jamie’s father separated, she said. They later divorced.

Advertisement

Jamie, who took his mother’s surname, recalled “odd experiences” when he was young, like when his mother joined him for father-son breakfasts at his primary school. But family was important – his maternal grandparents, John and Sarah Beaton, lived with them – and so was education. Jamie’s grandfather, a tradesman, always seemed to be leafing through a newspaper or an Andy McNab thriller. Related Article Billionaires The family feud over the $65 billion Ray-Ban fortune “Academics was our religion,” Jamie said. His mother said that one of her goals had been to expose her son to myriad opportunities. So he played tennis and basketball. He went camping, swimming, kayaking. He was nine when his mother introduced him to a chess coach named Glenn Harry Kwok. Kwok and Paula soon began dating and are now long-term partners. “I wondered why we weren’t doing much chess,” Jamie said.

Advertisement

His mother chauffeured him to tutoring centres and hired academic coaches, which was unusual for a middle-class family in New Zealand. “We wouldn’t be getting new cars or anything like that,” Paula Beaton said. “Everything revolved around education, and we didn’t see it as a sacrifice.” As a teenager, Jamie dreamed of attending a top college in the United States. In his final year of high school, he took more than twice the number of required courses. He was admitted to 25 universities, including Harvard, Yale and Princeton. Beaton and wife Priscilla are based in New York. NYT Before leaving home, he co-founded the counselling service that would become Crimson Education, billing it as a way to help international students navigate their way to US universities. After all, he had done it himself.

Advertisement

At Harvard, he felt all alone at first. Then he joined 15 student organisations, including the debate club and the undergraduate economics association. Brett Davis, one of Beaton’s roommates at Harvard, grew accustomed to his 2am business calls. “That was certainly a clue that this guy was thinking beyond the script of what is normal to do or achieve in college,” Davis said. Beaton was a sophomore when he emailed Julian Robertson, the founder of Tiger Management, a Wall Street hedge fund. Following a practice he had used with other traders at his firm, Robertson sent him off to be evaluated by a psychoanalyst – “Good fun,” Beaton said – before bringing him on board. Between classes at Harvard, Beaton spent two days a week at the Tiger Management offices in New York. Robertson, who died in 2022, and his son Alex, who now runs the firm, became mentors. Tiger Management was an early investor in Crimson Education. Alex Robertson recalled urging Beaton to have more work-life balance: Why not spend a week in Cancun with his buddies? “Honestly, Alex,” Beaton told him, “I can’t think of anything worse than sitting on a beach for five days when I want to work.”

Advertisement

Beaton was among the dozens of students who took a class on entrepreneurship taught by David Ager, a senior lecturer at Harvard Business School. Beaton stood out, not only because of his prominent spot in the amphitheatre – “In the front, three rows up,” Ager said – but also because he was such an active participant. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires The billionaire brat pack can’t stop whingeing. They’re only embarrassing themselves Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor “I say this with love,” Ager said, “but I’m sure there was a little bit of frustration that he had to share the time with other people.” Throughout his journey, Beaton has juggled academics and business. Belkin recalled that he often had his laptop open during class to check work emails or his stock portfolio. “Yet everything came in on time,” Belkin said. Beaton was multitasking in other ways, too, often talking with the student seated next to him, Priscilla Putzer. “There was a lot of whispering and giggling,” Belkin said.

Advertisement

Beaton and Putzer were married in April at a ceremony on the beach in Santa Monica, California. A company grows Crimson Education has not been immune from criticism. Early on, it faced pushback for using aggressive sales tactics and employing many college students as tutors and counsellors. As the company grew, Beaton said, it shifted to employing more full-time counsellors – the company now has 1200 full-time staff members, he said – and hired an accounting firm to vet its numbers. Of the 10,000 students who have used its services, more than 2000 have been accepted by Ivy League universities, Stanford or the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, he said. The company has also found itself the subject of a broader critique – that its high price tag effectively self-selects students who already have a good chance of getting into elite universities.

Advertisement

Jeff Selingo, a journalist who has written several books about college admissions, said that private counsellors can be a helpful resource for those who can afford them. “But it’s not going to get you into a place that you can’t get into otherwise,” he said. “I love the action, and I love a jam-packed day. It’s good fun.” Jamie Beaton Hamish Coates, an education expert at the Australian National University and Beaton’s thesis adviser at Tsinghua University, praised Beaton as someone who understood “the power of higher education”. But Coates posed a hypothetical: “Do you really want your child to be grooming themselves for the Ivy League from the age of five, when 95 per cent fail to get in? Or are you better off doing some finger painting, reading Frog and Toad and having a good life?” Beaton has heard that argument before – the “pressure-cooker environment” on one side and the “chill, happy childhood” on the other. He doesn’t buy the premise. “The students who try harder in high school are often the happiest and most engaged,” he said. His own future appears to be a work in progress. For now, he said, he is focused on “education and entrepreneurship”, along with starting a family. But several of his friends said they could see him entering politics. He has worked with New Zealand’s centre-right National Party, which was once headed by Key.

Advertisement

“If you said to me, ‘In 35 years’ time, Jamie will still be the CEO of Crimson’, I don’t see it,” Key said. “I think he’s got other, bigger things that he’s going to move on to.” Related Article Putin's Russia Billionaire gives Moscow the middle finger after being placed on Russia’s most wanted list At the end of his busy day, Beaton and his Crimson Education colleagues met with teenagers and their parents in a wood-paneled room of the Harvard Club. As servers passed around hors d’oeuvres, he stood before the group as a living advertisement for his company, the one-time whiz kid who had beaten the system. At one point Beaton ceded the stage to a colleague who spoke about scholarships available to high school students, including the John Locke essay competition. “How many are familiar with John Locke?” she asked.

Advertisement

A single hand shot up from the front row. “Not you, Jamie,” she said. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

title: Joyous energy and raucous humour collide in this five-star gig
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian return to the Palais with If You’re Feeling Sinister

MUSIC: Cellist Pieter Wispelwey explores solo suites by Benjamin Britten

DANCE: Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring One Last Tree to La Mama

OPERA: Lyric Opera put on a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE: 7 Dances for 7 People is performed at Northcote Town Hall

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.

Advertisement

As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

MUSIC

Pieter Wispelwey with Piers Lane ★★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15 Pure genius. These two words arguably encapsulate the astonishing imagination behind the three solo suites that Benjamin Britten composed for the Russian cellist Mstislav Rostropovich between 1964 and 1971. Taking Bach’s fabled cello suites as a model, these tours de force remain revolutionary in pushing the instrument’s boundaries of timbre and texture. Pieter Wispelwey performs at Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15, 2026 Laura Manariti Over three evenings, Dutch cellist Pieter Wispelwey, long an ardent and persuasive exponent of these works, is performing programs centred around each suite. Prokofiev and Shostakovich were appropriate stablemates in the series opener, not least because Prokofiev wrote his Cello Sonata in C, Op. 119 for Rostropovich, but also that the cellist was part of the deep friendship and admiration shared between himself, Shostakovich and Britten.

Advertisement

Providing the first taste of Wispelwey’s chameleonic way with his 1760 Guadagnini cello, the Prokofiev ran the gamut of emotions, starting with its dark, sombre opening before flowering into rich lyricism, moments of childlike wonder and folkloric exuberance. Britten’s Cello Suite No. 1, Op. 72 was full of ear-bending marvels, including a witty, cleverly constructed fugue and an evocative march in which the masterly bouncing of the bow summoned up martial images. A stunning moto perpetuo led to the return of the imposing, unifying Canto. Few others would be capable of bringing this music alive so vibrantly and comprehensibly. Pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic Laura Manariti Wispelwey ensured Shostakovich’s Cello Sonata in D minor, Op. 40 brimmed over with fascinating detail; bringing richly burnished tone to the eerie opening melody and plaintive Largo, unerring technique to the manic second movement and cheeky playfulness to the finale. Here and in the Prokofiev, pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic. Setting aside the substandard printed program that doesn’t even list the movements of the works performed, don’t miss the remaining two opportunities to hear astounding music performed by musicians of genius.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

DANCE

Our Last Tree ★★★

La Mama, until September 18 Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring something we rarely see on Melbourne stages: unpretentiously referential contemporary dance. Their latest show, Our Last Tree, points us with a sort of guileless enthusiasm towards the green earth and its wonders. Nelipot Collective perform Our Last Tree as part of La Mama’s Hope Punk Climate Festival Darren Gill Sometimes the relentless self-reflexivity of our local choreographers – their unwillingness to make work about the world beyond the stage – can seem like a fear of artistic failure. Nelipot embrace that fear with an earnest, wilfully naive fable of loss and recovery. Certainly, their slightly manic smiles and touchy-feely involvement of the audience suggest a community-oriented performance. You can imagine them at a farmers’ market, amid haybales and squealing children munching on small-batch fudge.

Advertisement

And yet I find their evocation of the life of the forest compelling. What they do best here is suggest – with reaching, serpentine limbs – the way that forests envelop us completely, above and below and all around. The intimate stage at La Mama, further compressed by the placement of a cardboard tree along one side, suits these densely convolved bodies. They seem to fill the space completely, coiling themselves into any chink of vacancy. Composer and violist Andrea Breen accompanies the performance with catchy, rather grand melodic hooks, which she returns to between wandering passages. Her music suggests something rooted yet inexorably moving, a tree’s stillness alive with change. Her score also implies a fuller orchestration: I hear the ghosts of horns and oboes underneath it. And yet the exposed solo voice suggests kinship with the last tree. Haunting, effective and beautifully played. Other production elements are less impressive. The slime-green tulle and the cardboard trunk (endearingly ornamented with hand-drawn growth rings) suggest a production for children; I suspect a younger audience would respond well. Yes, the work could be called unsophisticated, but only if that also means a refreshing independence from convention, as well as the courage to approach their subject directly.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.

Advertisement

Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.

Advertisement

After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Arts Second strike planned by Arts Centre Melbourne employees The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

title: Nyadol Nyuon responds to criticism over 'no white culture' remarks
text:
IN BRIEF The lawyer says race and culture should not be conflated, arguing there is no single "white culture".

Nyuon previously began returning her OAM as part of what she called her "slow and certain" departure from Australia.

Lawyer and human rights advocate Nyadol Nyuon has defended her claim that there is "no white culture" after remarks she made turning a televised debate drew criticism.

Nyuon appeared on the ABC's National Forum on migration on Monday, where she rejected the idea Australia was historically monocultural and said she had "no intention of assimilating".

But she stressed that did not mean rejecting Australia, its laws or the country she says she "deeply" loves.

She argued that describing Australia as an "Anglo-Celtic culture" risked creating the impression there was a single "white culture" migrants were expected to adopt.

"There is Italian culture, there is French culture, there is Argentinian culture, but there is not this notion of sort of a white culture that is being threatened," Nyuon told the forum.

The discussion came amid a broader national debate about migration, multiculturalism and what it means to be Australian.

Following criticism of her remarks, Nyuon expanded on the argument in a social media post on her LinkedIn account.

'No white culture'

"Apparently, saying there is no white culture has offended some people," she wrote on Tuesday.

"There is no white culture as there is no black culture."

Nyuon argued that race and culture should not be treated as interchangeable, pointing to the cultural differences that exist between people who may otherwise be grouped together according to skin colour.

"Black is a colour, not a culture. There are Black people. There is Ethiopian culture," she wrote.

Nyuon also defended her argument that Australia had never been monocultural, pointing to the hundreds of First Nations that existed before colonisation as well as the long histories of Chinese migrants and Afghan cameleers in Australia.

A debate over belonging

During the forum, former deputy prime minister John Anderson argued there were legitimate concerns among Australians about social cohesion and whether some groups respected Australian culture and values.

Anderson described those values as including individual dignity, equality before the law and the separation of the secular and sacred.

Nyuon acknowledged Australians had a right to be concerned about threats to social cohesion but challenged the way the issue was being framed.

She argued the migration debate could become a proxy for conversations about race and questioned why a person's appearance should influence perceptions of their belonging.

"Whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," she said on Monday.

'I love this country'

Nyuon also spoke about her complicated relationship with Australia and her previously announced intention to begin the process of renouncing her Australian citizenship.

The lawyer, who was born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia after her family fled the Sudanese civil war, came to Australia as a teenager.

In April, Nyuon revealed she had written to the governor-general's office to begin returning the Medal of the Order of Australia she was awarded in 2022 for "service to human rights and refugee women".

"This is the first step in my slow and certain process of leaving Australia and releasing my connections to this country," she wrote at the time.

Nyuon said she remained "so grateful" to Australia and would "always be indebted to it", but linked her decision to her experiences with Victoria University and WorkSafe Victoria.

Nyuon resigned from Victoria University in 2025, after overseeing an $800,000 WorkSafe Victoria project aimed at preventing workplace gendered violence, which was plagued by delays, strained relationships and resourcing issues.

An independent evaluator later found instability and mismanagement meant it could not properly assess the program's success.

Speaking on National Forum, she said she loved Australia but was conscious that political circumstances could affect whether she and her children felt they could remain.

"Many migrants deeply, deeply love this country. I love this country," she said.

In her subsequent LinkedIn post, Nyuon maintained her comments about culture were not intended as an insult.

title: Tony Burke set to unveil Labor's new migration plan amid working holiday visa concerns
text:
In Brief Labor has previously proposed reducing net overseas migration and set a target of 225,000 arrivals a year by 2027-28.

Burke was initially scheduled to unveil the policy last month but it was pushed back.

Labor is expected to unveil its long-awaited migration policy, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke set to outline the plan at the National Press Club on Thursday.

The policy was initially due to be unveiled by Burke at a National Press Club address in August. However, the speech was cancelled at the last minute after the government failed to secure cabinet agreement on the best approach.

Since then, Labor has maintained it was still finalising its plans.

The announcement is expected to detail how Labor will reduce net overseas migration from about 300,000 in 2025 to 245,000 in 2026/27 and 225,000 per year thereafter.

It comes as migration has emerged as a key political battleground, with pressure mounting on Labor to release its strategy.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has repeatedly declined to provide further details, refusing to set a timeframe for migration announcements and saying they would be made at "appropriate times".

What could Labor be planning?

Labor has previously proposed reducing net overseas migration and set an annual target of 225,000 by 2027-28.

Burke has already flagged plans to make more changes to the visa system to curb net overseas migration, with the government officially confirming in August that it would slow the processing of working holiday visa applications.

The horticulture and tourism sectors have been calling for certainty, raising fears that a backlog of working holiday visas could mean there aren't enough workers for regional businesses in the summer months.

Labor is also expected to tighten rules for international students and their families and further restrict some visitor visas.

Potential changes could prevent international students from switching courses to extend their stay, increase scrutiny of onshore visa applications, limit the number of family members attached to student visas, and restrict transfers from higher education into vocational education and training programs.

Some tourist visas are also expected to be reduced from 12 months to six months.

The Albanese government has already confirmed that Australia's annual humanitarian intake of 20,000 places will not be reduced.

Burke has previously argued migration plans should be considered alongside housing supply, saying in June: "If you go at migration the wrong way, then you can actually make the housing situation worse."

Political pressure builds

Negotiations between the government and the Coalition over migration settings have stalled over the last week, with the Opposition pushing for deeper cuts to net overseas migration and stronger powers around deportation.

But both parties have criticised One Nation's plan revealed on Monday saying it would "shock" the economy and devastate the construction, health and aged care sectors.

One Nation proposed cutting temporary migration by more than 750,000 places over three years, arguing Australia's migration system requires a major "reset".

Under the policy, international students, recent graduates and their family members would be hit hardest, with migration places in those categories reduced by almost 470,000 over three years.

Burke has told SBS News he tried to find a path for bipartisan agreement with the Opposition.

"I had hoped that the Opposition would work constructively to make sure the immigration minister of the day had additional powers to be able to regulate net overseas migration," he said on Wednesday.

"At the moment, they haven't agreed to measures which they claim to support.

"I would much rather have more targeted levers available."

Independent ACT senator David Pocock took aim at Labor on Wednesday morning, saying current conversations about migration were "unproductive" and had to factor in what the country needed over the next 10 years.

"The big thing I would love to see is a plan," he told ABC's Radio National.

"There's this constant talk about numbers, about classes of visas, rather than actually having the conversation as a country — what is our 10-year plan for migration?"

It was those "hard conversations" that were paramount to Australia's migration debate, he argued.

"To me, that’s how you solve this issue ... rather than having this ridiculous fight over a number that raises all sorts of concerns for aged care, for healthcare, for farmers who are relying on backpackers."

"It just seems so unproductive."

The Coalition is yet to release its migration policy, but has hinted that its plan will tie migration figures to the amount of new homes built, which is currently tracking around 173,000 per year.

Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he was looking forward to seeing the detail of Labor's plan but was "deeply sceptical about Labor's ability to deliver, because for four years they've failed to deliver".

"As for our own policy, we are close to releasing it, but we're actually going to do the work to get it right because we are not the government," he told reporters in Canberra.

"We are seeking to be the government after the next election and we're not going to put out a half-baked policy like One Nation has that hasn't even been costed, the budgetary impacts of which they have no idea."

title: Four more acts quit Ed Sheeran tour as singer says Macklemore decision 'was not mine'
text:
IN BRIEF US rapper Macklemore said he was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour this week after making pro-Palestinian comments.

He said on Monday that several US venues had vowed to prohibit him from appearing as Sheeran's opening act.

Four supporting acts have quit Ed Sheeran's tour after the rapper Macklemore was removed for pro-Palestinian comments he made during a concert in New Jersey.

Hours after Sheeran posted on social media about Macklemore's removal and attributed the decision to the tour's promoters, Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, the Danish band Lukas Graham, and Finneas posted on Instagram that they would withdraw from Sheeran's tour.

Rowe was one of Macklemore's replacements for Sheeran's remaining US dates, while Beoga was serving as Sheeran's touring band. Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year.

Rowe and Beoga each cited their country's history in their statements explaining their decision.

"We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be," Beoga said.

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," the band posted, seemingly referring to billionaire Robert Kraft's role in Macklemore's removal from the tour.

Sheeran weighed in on Macklemore being dropped as his opening act after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments onstage during their tour, saying the decision was made by the promoters alone. The British singer also said he refused to be drawn into a public discussion about the war in Gaza.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran wrote on Instagram on Tuesday. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

Sheeran's statement came a day after Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after exclaiming "Free Palestine!" during the 5 September date at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium while introducing his protest song Hind's Hall.

title: Profits in Australia's property market still 'exceptionally high' despite recent downturn
text:
IN BRIEF New data from Cotality shows that 95.4 per cent of dwelling sales made a gain in the June quarter.

While dwelling values declined over the quarter, prices remained significantly higher than six years earlier.

Australia is undergoing one of the steepest housing downturns in decades, but years of strong growth mean most homes are still being sold for a hefty profit.

In the June quarter, 95.4 per cent of dwelling sales made a gain, down from the 21-year high of 96.1 per cent recorded in the three months to March, research from data provider Cotality showed on Wednesday.

While national dwelling values declined 1.5 per cent over the June quarter, prices were still more than 67 per cent higher than six years earlier.

Several years of very strong growth had left many home owners with a substantial equity buffer, helping vendors rake in a combined $35.9 billion in profit in the quarter, Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.

"Profitability is still exceptionally high by historical standards, but we are starting to see the impact of weaker housing market conditions flow through to resale outcomes," Burg said.

"Most sellers are still benefiting from the significant value growth accumulated over the past five years, which is providing considerable protection against the early stages of the downturn.

"With home values falling across more markets, that buffer will become increasingly important in determining resale outcomes."

Australia's housing downturn continued to deepen in July and August, as the outlook for interest rates worsened and investors continued to count the cost of the federal government's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains discount.

READ MORE Why Australia's richest suburbs could be a warning for every homeowner

Nationwide prices are only down 3.6 per cent from their March peak, but several economists, including at HSBC and Morgan Stanley, expect the total fall in values to hit 10 per cent or more, which would be the deepest downturn in more than 40 years.

The pace of the decline has also rattled sentiment, with the 2022/23 downturn the only time prices have fallen faster for longer since the 1980s.

Buyers who held onto their property for a longer period of time were better able to ride out the cyclical ebbs and flows.

"Owners who have held their property for nine or 10 years have generally experienced several periods of value growth, giving them a much larger equity buffer when market conditions weaken," Burg said.

Houses that sold for a profit were held for a median 9.3 years, compared with the typical holding time of 4.4 years for loss-making house resales.

Overall, 97.8 per cent of houses were sold for a profit, underscoring the growth advantage of freestanding homes over units. Only 90.5 per cent of unit sales made a profit.

Sydney was still the top money spinner in dollar terms, with a total profit of $6.6 billion.

But the proportion of sales that made a profit eased to 92.7 per cent, well below Brisbane, which recorded a profit in 99.8 per cent of sales.

Nationally, the median gain eased from a record $378,000 to $371,000, while the median loss increased from $44,000 to $45,000.

title: 'Won't back away': Hanson's partial apology to Indigenous Australians and Albanese

title: Want a comfortable retirement? Here's the new super figure Australians need
text:
IN BRIEF Goods and services that retirees spend most on rise faster than inflation, a peak body says.

A comfortable retirement is becoming more expensive as a result.

Australians now need a little bit more in their super to retire comfortably, with the rising cost of living driving up the latest retirement standard.

A couple who own their home and are seeking a comfortable retirement will need $78,998 a year, or $1,513 a week. A single homeowner will need $56,166 a year, or $1,076 a week.

Those figures were released on Tuesday by the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), the peak body for the super industry.

It showed for homeowners aged 65 to 84, the budget for a comfortable retirement rose 0.5 per cent for couples and 0.4 per cent for singles in the June quarter.

For a modest retirement, their budget rose 0.4 per cent for couples and 0.3 per cent for singles, to $52,690 and $36,548 a year respectively.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

For retirees aged 85 and over, a comfortable retirement will cost $74,484 per year for couples and $53,964 per year for singles. For retirees who rent privately, a modest budget is now $69,376 per year for a couple and $51,418 per year for a single.

ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty says retirees are being affected by the soaring cost of living more than others because the things they buy are rising quicker than the inflation rate of 3.8 per cent.

These include electricity, which the group said rose 22.4 per cent after federal and state rebates ended (22 per cent), car costs (6.5 per cent), medical services (5 per cent), insurance (almost 5 per cent) and meals out (4 per cent).

Source: SBS News

"Retirees are among the groups hit hardest by the cost of living crisis because their budgets are weighted towards the things going up in price the most," Delahunty said.

What's a comfortable retirement compared to a modest one?

AFSA defines a comfortable retirement as being able to afford quality private health insurance, eat out most weeks, and go on a yearly holiday in Australia or overseas every few years.

A modest retirement includes basic health cover, such as a hospital-only plan, domestic-only holidays, and occasional eating out.

On the age pension alone, it's a much slimmer budget with limited lifestyle and basic living spending.

"Most of these things drop out of your budget entirely," ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty said.

She said while the age pension goes up with inflation, it doesn't allow for spending on other things like private health and holidays, which are increasing in price, and leaving retirees more reliant on their super to make those payments.

"Super is the difference between watching every dollar and having a sense of financial security in retirement," Delahunty said.

READ MORE How much super do Australians need to retire? It could be less than you think

Superannuation as an election issue

As Australia nears a federal election, superannuation has become a major political campaign line as the parties try to win voters amid a cost of living crisis.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers signalled super could become a political issue at the next federal election, and accused his political opponents of trying to "end compulsory superannuation as we know it".

His calls came after Liberal senator Andrew Bragg declared superannuation an "illiberal experiment".

One Nation has proposed allowing workers paying rent or a mortgage to divert 3 per cent of their super payments straight to their wallet for up to three years — investing only 9 per cent instead of the current compulsory rate of 12 per cent.

READ MORE Labor reveals super increase position amid 'predatory' practices crackdown

The policy has come under criticism from super firms and the government, with some estimates that people opting into the scheme could lose $25,000 from their retirement fund.

ASFA calculates a similar loss, saying a 30-year-old on average full-time earnings who takes three years of super as cash under the One Nation proposal would receive around $54 a week now and retire with $23,900 less in today's dollars.

"The cost of living and housing crises need their own solutions. Forcing Australians to solve them by robbing from their own future selves is not a helping hand. It is a worse deal than previous generations had," Delahunty said.

title: Could a Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish independence pact threaten UK unity?
text:
In brief The Scottish National Party, Wales' Plaid Cymru and the pro-Irish unity Sinn Féin want to break away from the UK.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously rejected Northern Ireland or Scotland holding referendums on the matter.

Leaders of the main Scottish, Northern Irish and Welsh nationalist parties declared at a meeting overnight that they have the right to choose whether to stay in the United Kingdom, with all three seeing their future as nations within the European Union.

The Scottish National Party (SNP), Plaid Cymru in Wales, and the pro-Irish-unity Sinn Féin want to break away from the UK, although under different timelines and conditions.

The rare meeting in the Welsh capital came just days after United States President Donald Trump waded in on the issue, saying he would back a united Ireland.

His comments showed "the unity debate is very much alive", Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill said alongside fellow party leaders as they announced a memorandum of understanding.

"Our nations have the right to self-determination. No Westminster government (the UK government) has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future," the agreement said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SNP leader John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, leader of Plaid Cymru in Wales, and Mary Lou McDonald and O'Neill, leader and deputy leader of Sinn Féin, met in their roles as party leaders, rather than as top officials in their respective governments.

O'Neill is Northern Ireland's first minister while Iorwerth and Swinney lead their respective nationalist parties in Scotland and Wales.

Where do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland stand on the independence issue?

The agreement said that, for the first time, each nation had a first minister "committed to independence from the UK", adding: "The future of our nations belongs in the European Union."

The independence parties are the biggest in both the Scottish and Welsh parliaments for the first time since devolution measures began in 1999. Sinn Féin has been the biggest party in Northern Ireland's assembly since 2022.

The SNP wants a second independence referendum after an earlier ballot in 2014 saw Scotland narrowly vote to remain in Britain. Successive UK governments have ruled out an immediate rerun.

Sinn Féin, the former political wing of the paramilitary Irish Republican Army (IRA), wants a vote on the UK territory of Northern Ireland being reunified with Ireland.

Plaid Cymru seeks Welsh independence in the longer term, but Iorwerth has ruled out pressing for a referendum immediately.

Could an independence move succeed?

Laura McAllister, a politics professor at Cardiff University, said the deliberately broad term "self-determination" was used due to these differing timelines and goals.

"Plaid Cymru was elected with heavy emphasis on avoiding the issue of independence this term," she told Agence France-Presse (AFP).

Shortly after taking power, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Irish unity was "off the table".

The 1998 Good Friday peace agreement that largely ended three decades of conflict in Northern Ireland provides for a referendum if Westminster's Northern Ireland minister believes a majority is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.

Sinn Féin leader McDonald said the prime minister had no authority to deny any provisions of the agreement, and Burnham backtracked in parliament last week.

On Monday, a spokesperson insisted that Burnham believed "strongly in the Union", the constitutional tie that makes Northern Ireland part of the UK.

On Scotland, Burnham told lawmakers there could be another vote if there was a "clear consensus" but later reportedly said a referendum remained "off limits".

"It is unlikely that this (meeting) will change the UK Government's refusal to allow a referendum in Scotland or, at present, Northern Ireland," said Michael Keating, an emeritus politics professor at the University of Aberdeen.

But the meeting was "significant politically", he told AFP, because the other parties long avoided association with Sinn Féin due to its link to the IRA.

Alex Kane, a former communications chief for Ireland's Ulster Unionist Party, pointed to the absence of Northern Ireland's deputy first minister, Emma Little-Pengelly, of the pro-UK Democratic Unionist Party.

Her post is of equal weight to O'Neill's under Belfast's power-sharing government and "neither can claim to represent the government of Northern Ireland if the other hasn't agreed to it," he told AFP.

Little-Pengelly slammed O'Neill, claiming her position was "weaponised" at "a summit of separatists".

The meeting sparked mixed reactions in Belfast.

"Ireland would be better off if it was one country and we were back in the EU," retiree Ray Dennison, 61, told AFP.

But Jim Boyle, a 64-year-old environmental worker, said the meeting filled him with "trepidation".

"Many years ago I may have wished for the break-up of the United Kingdom, now ... I just don't want anything that's unpredictable."

title: 'Enormously confronting': The uncomfortable truth behind the HYROX defecation controversy
text:
In brief An Australian athlete was pictured with faeces on her legs during a HYROX race in China.

The incident has drawn heated debate about the rules of the competition.

It was an incident that triggered international headlines. But while a HYROX athlete's mid-race bowel movement has raised questions about hygiene and fairness, the urge to go is a familiar reality for many endurance athletes.

HYROX is a fitness and endurance race that combines 8km of running with exercises such as rowing, sled pushes and wall balls, carried out in indoor exhibition halls.

The co-founder of the global sport, Moritz Fürste, apologised on Monday after Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk soiled herself during a race in Beijing over the weekend and went on to win.

Footage posted on social media showed Wietrzyk, who holds the sport's women's solo pro world record, competing at stations with faeces on her legs.

"I apologise to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have," Fürste's statement said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race."

Fürste said the organisation had immediately begun improving its event processes and had introduced new rules and procedures to prevent a similar situation from occurring again.

The incident triggered significant backlash online, with some arguing it had affected other racers' ability to compete in a safe and hygienic environment.

Joanna Wietrzyk is the world record holder in the HYROX women's solo event. Source: Getty / VCG

"These competitors pay hundreds of dollars to participate and spend weeks, if not months, training for these events. Their health, safety, and ability to perform should matter just as much as anyone else's," read one comment which received thousands of likes.

Critics also questioned why officials did not intervene, given HYROX imposes penalties for other acts such as spitting and nostril clearing.

Gut issues and endurance sports

It's not unusual for endurance athletes to experience gastrointestinal symptoms during competition, nor is it unheard of for them to continue despite soiling themselves.

During the 2005 London Marathon, eventual winner Paula Radcliffe stopped and relieved herself in view of TV cameras.

She later explained she had been running through stomach cramps — likely affecting her speed — because of her reluctance to relieve herself in front of "however many thousands of people were watching on television".

READ MORE The secret to good gut health? It starts with eating the rainbow

French race walker Yohann Diniz experienced intestinal issues during the 2016 Olympics, but continued walking for many kilometres despite soiling himself.

According to research by Monash University, strenuous exercise lasting two hours or more — particularly running — appears to exacerbate gut disturbances.

Researchers estimate 30 to 70 per cent of athletes experience gastrointestinal symptoms, with endurance athletes particularly susceptible.

Bec Hoschke, a former professional triathlete and Ironman champion who now coaches endurance athletes in Sydney, told SBS News gut health can be a "highly sensitive thing for many endurance athletes".

The HYROX Beijing event was held over the weekend. Source: Getty / Fred Lee

She said the HYROX incident was a "very difficult situation" for the parties involved: the competition, the athlete and her competitors.

"Athletes make enormous sacrifices for international competition," she said. "For some athletes, it's their living."

She said the issue was not only one of public health and hygiene but also of the health and well-being of the athlete involved.

"I can't imagine the mental impact all of this is having on someone. I think she's only in her early 20s as well. It's enormously confronting for someone to have to deal with at that age."

Wietrzyk reportedly posted on her Instagram story after the race showing herself attached to an IV, writing "go hard or go home they say ... a win is a win", but later deleted the post.

Her coach, Chris Bayens, said what had happened was "extraordinary", "unforeseen" and difficult to comprehend in real time.

"Decisions were made under competition conditions by an athlete, judges and officials, all responding to a situation none of them could reasonably have prepared for," he wrote in an Instagram post.

He said discussion and review of those decisions was legitimate, but "the hatred and personal attacks that have followed are not".

"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human."

Hoschke said HYROX presents different considerations to more individualised endurance events like marathon running because athletes compete in a contained space and use shared equipment.

"I hope that the public and the people that are involved in the sport can get something out of this conversation for the benefit of the sport," she said.

title: 'New low': Zali Steggall weighs in on controversial Sydney Sweeney ad
text:
IN BRIEF US actress Sydney Sweeney is facing criticism from Australian athletes over a new ad.

Sweeney is being accused of belittling women's sports with the campaign for a betting company.

Independent MP and former Olympian Zali Steggall has criticised a new sexualised sports betting advertisement featuring United States actress Sydney Sweeney as a "new low", amid mounting uproar over its depiction of women in sport.

In her latest controversial ad, Sweeney features naked in the ad for a sports betting company — in some scenes her private parts covered only by footballs or other sports gear.

"They wanted to show just sports," she says while sitting topless on a basketball hoop, before repeatedly saying "sports" in other suggestive poses.

The ad has sparked backlash from current and former female athletes around the world, outraged by its portrayal of women in sport. Some, including Australian water poloist Matilda Kearns, have taken to social media to show "real" women in sport.

Kearns posted a video of her competing in the pool and training at the gym with the caption: "Here's some real women sports content."

Retired Australian swimming champion Ariarne Titmus said the ad was "a kick in the face" to women who'd dedicated their lives to perfecting their craft.

Four-time Olympic gold medallist Ariarne Titmus is the reigning Olympic champion in the women's 400m freestyle. Source: AAP / Jason O'Brien

"I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this," she said in a since-expired social media post.

"How do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing? To take the mickey like this, I thought we were genuinely moving past this bullsh-t."

Steggall, Australia's most successful alpine skier, described the gambling ad as "incredibly disappointing and just offensive".

"It uses a woman's body to sell sports betting while reducing women's sport to a sexualised punchline. It's a trope that we need to do away with and it comes from an industry already targeting young men through sports to gamble to ruin their lives," Steggall said.

She said as a young athlete she was often pressured to do sexualised campaigns showing her body in ways that made her uncomfortable, and "really cheapened me as an athlete".

Zali Steggall is Australia's most successful alpine skier, having performed in four Winter Olympics between 1992 and 2002. Source: AP / David Phillip

"Female athletes have fought for decades to be recognised for what we are, serious competitive athletes — strong and powerful," the MP for the Sydney seat of Warringah said in a social media post.

Steggall appealed to young girls, saying her Olympian's body is strong and powerful and she was proud of what her body was capable of.

"It doesn't look like what Sydney Sweeney and others show. It comes in all shapes and sizes.

"To young men — don't be fooled, this is a gambling company trying to lure you using sex to get your attention so they can lose their money."

It's not the first time Sweeney has courted controversy for an ad. Last year, she was accused of promoting white supremacy after featuring in a campaign for denim brand US Eagle, which featured the tagline, "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans". In the ad, she discussed biological traits passed down from parents.

Sweeney featured in a number of poses naked or partially naked in the advertisement for gambling. Credit: Supplied

Gender Equity Victoria CEO Micaela Drieberg said it was infuriating to see women's bodies sexualised for the sake of gambling.

"It flies in the face of every hard-fought win for women athletes, and reinforces a gender stereotype that women's bodies are there to sell commodities," she told SBS News.

Drieberg said it perpetuates an unacceptable view that this is how women's bodies should be portrayed and used, and it "adds years" to the fight for gender equality.

"It's been incredible to watch the evolution of women in sports and the respect that athletes have and deserve increase year on and year out.

"When we see campaigns like this ... it puts us back."

title: 'Hoax': Donald Trump dismisses warnings that AI could destroy humanity
text:
In brief Tech leaders have urged regulations requiring independent audits of advanced frontier AI models.

Trump, in a post on social media, said the industry's call for regulation is a "hoax".

United States President Donald Trump has dismissed fears that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity, calling them a hoax and rejecting global calls to put guardrails around the fast-moving technology.

Trump's pushback comes amid growing international alarm about AI, with even some tech bosses saying development of computer super-intelligence needs to slow down.

Trump said the US could not afford to lose a technological race with rival China and insisted the only guardrails necessary were a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," Trump said in one of a series of posts on his Truth Social network about the subject.

Trump compared it to what he called "all the other hoaxes", including the investigation into ties between his election campaign and Russia, and his impeachment over Ukraine, both in his first term.

Earlier, Trump alleged what he called a "SICK conspiracy" against AI and attacked "Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers" who opposed the technology.

The US leader also lashed out at Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, who called on Saturday for AI companies to ease the pace of development, and at other firms.

"The Trump Administration has stopped AI 'people' from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,' like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel'," the US president wrote.

Trump — who has made AI data centres central to his economic plans — questioned why AI firms want regulation that "will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy."

He also trained his fire on Google, urging it to rethink plans for a US$15 billion ($21 billion) AI investment in Finland, which he blamed on "finding permitting too difficult in the United States".

But the 80-year-old Republican faces a growing backlash from US voters amid the mounting fears that AI could wipe out humanity by creating pathogens or triggering nuclear war.

A majority of people in the US are also opposed to energy-guzzling AI data centres, which have become a major issue in crucial US midterm elections in November.

Amodei — whose firm Anthropic makes the hugely successful AI system Claude — was quickly backed by OpenAI boss Sam Altman and by former Trump ally Elon Musk, who also owns xAI.

The latest warnings were sparked after OpenAI developers reported scares in which AI models broke out of what were supposed to be secure testing spaces, reached the internet and coordinated to attack Hugging Face, a site where code is stored.

Global concerns about AI and a possible extinction event have dramatically escalated in recent days.

The UN Security Council will hold a meeting on artificial intelligence next week amid growing international concern, a French diplomatic source said on Monday.

United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk called on Monday for countries and artificial intelligence companies to act urgently to rein in a technology he warned posed "unprecedented risks".

Britain's King Charles will host representatives of leading AI firms for a gathering in Scotland, a source close to the event said on Monday, as the worries mount.

title: 'A lot of work to be done': Australia's major health win faces its next challenge
text:
IN BRIEF HIV diagnoses have fallen significantly in Australia since 2016.

Experts say more equity in testing, prevention and treatment is needed for some groups.

HIV diagnoses have fallen significantly over the past decade, with Australia on track to achieve preliminary UN targets as part of a world-leading response, but experts say progress remains uneven across communities.

The latest Australian HIV and sexually transmitted infection data show that, overall, HIV diagnoses in Australia have fallen 25 per cent in a decade.

From 2016 to 2025, there was a 28 per cent decline in HIV diagnoses among males, and no change among women, a feature of the data attributed to high rates of testing, treatment and use of pre-exposure prophylaxis medicine, known as PrEP, among men who have sex with men.

Australia is a signatory to the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), which leads the global effort to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

Currently in Australia, 94 per cent of people living with HIV have been diagnosed, 95 per cent of HIV-positive people are receiving treatment. Of that figure, 98 per cent of treatments have resulted in suppressing HIV to undetectable and virtually untransmittable levels.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While it is expected Australia will achieve the preliminary UNAIDS targets, where 95 per cent of people living with HIV are diagnosed, 95 per cent of those diagnosed are on treatment, and 95 per cent of those on treatment have HIV that is virally suppressed, analysis from the Kirby Institute at the University of New South Wales has shown that some groups are being left behind.

What does the data show?

The HIV notification rate — a figure that accounts for the change in growing populations — showed that the overall rate of HIV notification per 100,000 people had dropped from approximately 4 in 2016 to just under 3 in 2025.

The notification rate was seven times higher among males than females in Australia.

Overall, Australia had a 28 per cent reduction in HIV diagnoses between 2016 and 2025. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

In 2025, the transmission of the majority of HIV cases was attributed to male-to-male sexual contact, at 64 per cent, while 26 per cent were attributed to heterosexual sexual contact, and a small proportion, 3 per cent, were attributed to injection drug use.

Rates of HIV remain low among people who inject drugs in Australia and among sex workers, which Kirby Institute epidemiologist Dr Skye McGregor said reflected the strong and long-running community response to HIV among priority populations.

The groups falling behind

The most recent period, 2025, saw the highest number of HIV diagnoses in First Nations peoples, with 3.9 notifications per 100,000 — 1.9 times the diagnosis rate for Australian-born non-Indigenous people.

McGregor said this reflected a need to work closely with communities to ensure prevention, treatment and testing responses were appropriate.

Experts said it was important to ensure that messaging around testing, prevention and treatment was accessible, to ensure no groups are left behind as Australia achieves HIV targets. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

More than half of gay and bisexual men diagnosed with HIV were born overseas, and from 2016-2025, while diagnoses among gay and bisexual men born in Australia reduced by 48 per cent, for those born overseas, that figure was only 18 per cent.

Scientia professor at the Kirby Institute, professor Andrew Grulich, said that while there have been significant advancements in self-testing and other outreach activities such as the installation of HIV testing vending machines in universities, equity in care was the next challenge.

"When we look at the data, we find reductions in HIV are not as good outside of the city as they are in the city. We need better access to testing and to PrEP outside of the city centres," he said.

While the number of HIV diagnoses was higher for men than women, diagnoses for men declined over a ten-year period, while that figure for women remained the same. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

President of the National Association of People with HIV, Scott Harlum, said Australia was in a good position to confront these issues head-on.

"In Australia we do this better than anywhere else in the world, that's our track record. We have the best people in the world; we have a government that's committed to it; nothing is lacking.

"But there are disparities in these numbers that are only going to be answered by speaking to these communities, especially for new arrivals to the country."

Late diagnosis of HIV was also an emerging issue: in 2025, one-third of diagnoses were considered "late", which often meant someone had been living with undiagnosed HIV for four years.

McGregor from the Kirby Institute said there was a clear need for a range of testing strategies that are accessible for all populations, including Australian-born and overseas-born populations, adding that HIV tests should be normalised as a regular part of sexual health.

"We're lucky to have self-testing in Australia, but we also need accessible healthcare and clinician education, so when someone goes for a sexual health checkup, it should include HIV and gonorrhoea," she said.

Jessica Michaels, deputy chief financial officer at the Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine, said there was "a lot of work to be done" around stigma and discrimination reduction, especially for healthcare workers, who she said were still discussing prevention and testing with people "based on preconceived ideas of who is at risk".

"We really need to move away from that, and to have all healthcare workers thinking 'could it be HIV?' regardless of who is sitting in front of them."

title: Labor appoints former Liberal leader Sussan Ley to Snowy Hydro board role
text:
In brief Labor has tapped former Liberal Party leader Sussan Ley to join the board of the Snowy Hydro 2.0 project.

Many Snowy workers live in Ley's former electorate of Farrer.

A former coalition leader has been appointed by the Labor government to help steer the nation's most expensive and delayed renewable energy project.

Sussan Ley will sit on the Snowy Hydro board following her resignation from politics earlier this year, Climate Minister Chris Bowen announced on Monday.

The wholly government-owned project includes eight power stations and more than a dozen dams, spanning more than 100 kilometres from Thredbo to Tumut in NSW's south.

Snowy 2.0 is now being built and will store excess power from wind and solar, intended to become the centrepiece of the project.

Ley quit politics in February after being deposed by Angus Taylor as opposition leader, ending a 24-year career. She then took a reflective road trip around the United States, absorbing the sights of little-travelled areas on Greyhound buses.

Now, it is time for her to begin again — this time by tackling one of the country's most controversial projects.

Snowy 2.0, in the NSW Kosciuszko National Park, is seven years behind schedule. Costs have so far ballooned to $12 billion from an initial $2 billion budget and are expected to grow further.

It faced scrutiny for safety issues and hefty executive bonuses despite missing targets.

Ley's previous electorate of Farrer takes in the Murrumbidgee, Murray River and Albury, where many Snowy workers live.

She is being appointed alongside Merryn York, who has worked extensively on engineering technology.

"Their combined knowledge and skill will help Snowy Hydro deliver reliable power, stronger regional economies and more Australian jobs," Bowen said.

The women will replace outgoing board members Sandra Dodds and Scott Mitchell.

It is not the first time a Labor government has appointed a former Liberal politician to a government role. Previous NSW energy minister Matt Kean was named as the chair of the Climate Change Authority in 2024.

title: ‘It’s time to move on’: NRLW greats Elliott and Baxter call time on careers
text:

SportNRLNRLW 2026 ‘It’s time to move on’: NRLW greats Elliott and Baxter call time on careers Billie Eder Updated September 16, 2026 — 2:27pm ,first published September 13, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
