There are few people more influential in women’s rugby league than Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter, which is why it felt like the end of an era when the Roosters duo announced they’d both be retiring from the game at the end of 2026. The news, while unexpected, was unsurprising from Baxter who, at 32 years old, has already made a comeback to the game twice – the first after giving birth to her second son Beauden in 2022, and the second after she ruptured her ACL in 2024. Corban Baxter with her sons Carter and Beauden. James Brickwood “I probably struggled the last couple of years, returning from my ACL,” Baxter said. “I think my body’s started to slow down. I’ve tried to push through that probably the last couple of seasons, and then obviously having a young family, it’s a lot of time away from them, and I’ve been doing it for the whole life of my 15-year-old son [Carter].

Advertisement

“It was a bit of a family decision too, to make sure that I can have more time with them, but it was something that wasn’t solidified until probably earlier on in this season.” Elliott’s announcement came as much more of a shock. The 28-year-old made her return to the game this year after having her first child Gigi, and went straight into the NSW Blues Origin side that won the series 3-0. Millie Elliott with her husband Adam, their daughter Gigi and his son Lenny. James Brickwood As Roosters coach John Strange said on Wednesday, both Baxter and Elliott are at the top of their game and remain pivotal parts of his undefeated Tricolours team that is eyeing a third grand final appearance in three years. “I just knew that it was time for me,” Elliott said. “I’ve always played because I love the game. And, you know, women’s rugby league players that are playing right now are playing because they genuinely love the game and I still really love the game.

Advertisement

“I’ve only just thought about this in the last six to eight weeks, and that’s something that I’ve had to process with and chat to the girls with. It’s never been something that I’ve thought of before, and I feel really content with what I’ve achieved in rugby league. “Having my daughter Gigi and being able to bring her along the ride this year has been very special, but it’s time to move on for that next chapter of my career and life ... I just knew myself that I was ready.” Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter announce their retirement from rugby league. James Brickwood The term trailblazer is one that gets thrown around too often in rugby league, but for these two women the title certainly rings true. They’ve been there from the start. Elliott became the first NRLW player to win four premierships when she lifted the trophy with the Tricolours in 2024, after previously doing it with Newcastle in 2022 and Brisbane in 2019 and 2020. She’s also won the Origin shield four times with NSW.

Advertisement

Baxter was the first Roosters captain to lift the NRLW premiership trophy for the club in 2021, and she was in the NSW team that won four Origin titles between 2016 and 2019. Both have been pioneers of the women’s game, which has grown from a four-round competition in 2018 to 12 teams in 2026, and now includes a reserve-grade competition that runs alongside the NRLW season. Roosters captain Corban Baxter poses with the Premiership trophy after her team’s victory over the Dragons in the 2021 NRLW grand final. Getty Images “When the competition came in, let’s be honest, no one really cared – I’m not sugarcoating it,” Elliott said. “The comp was very small, I guess a little bit, I don’t want to say tokenistic, but we played each other once, and there were four teams. It was a very short comp.

Advertisement

“But the fact we’re sitting here in a press conference room, we’ve got State of Origin where we have thousands [attend], millions of people tune in to watch it on television in prime-time slots... “The fact that we go to a footy game, and people know who we are, that’s just crazy. I really want to give credit to the people in rugby league who profile the women’s game. It’s changed our lives, and it’s crazy to think what it’s going to do for this next generation of players coming through. ” Both retiring stars are calling time on rugby league to focus on their family and the next chapter in their careers. Both already have roles in the media – Elliott with Nine, the publisher of this masthead, while Baxter appears on Fox’s NRLW coverage and also does some coaching. To bow out with one more premiership for the Roosters would be the cherry on top.

Advertisement

“We would love to finish on a high and get that premiership with the girls,” Baxter said. “Retiring or not, that’s the goal. We want to win premierships, and we’ve done our reflections on last year, the fire is well and truly burning within, as a team. “To go out on a high would be a dream come true.” ‘They can be beaten’: Undefeated Roosters aren’t a sure thing for title, says V’landys As the NRLW finals get under way this week, the 2026 premiership appears to be a two-horse race between the Roosters and the Titans.

Advertisement

The Roosters are undefeated this season and have a week off before the preliminary finals next weekend, while the Titans, who also have a week off, have only lost once this year – their round one match against the Tricolours. Roosters NRLW captain Isabelle Kelly is ready for another finals campaign. Oscar Colman It sets up a potentially mouth-watering decider, with last year’s premiers Brisbane the only team seemingly capable of stopping the top two. ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys conceded the Roosters’ dominance may not be good for the women’s competition – they have only lost three games in the past three years, and their most recent defeat was to Brisbane in the 2025 grand final – but he is confident teams are capable of stepping up to end their streak. “Look, it isn’t [a good thing], but the thing is that they can be beaten,” V’landys said.

Advertisement

“As I’ve learnt in the racing industry, a favourite can be beaten, and I think there are a few more teams there that will give the Roosters an absolute run for their money. “So, I don’t think it’s going to be as dominant as what the season’s been – the semi-finals go to another level.” The Tricolours go into their week off fit and healthy, a welcome change from last year when halfback Tarryn Aiken damaged her ACL just before the finals. The Roosters have been unstoppable in 2026. Getty Images The pain of last year’s grand final, which the Broncos won via a 65th minute try to Mele Hufanga, is still fresh in the mind of Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly. And while the team is undefeated in 2026 – something Kelly is adamant they have not spoken about – she is under no illusions that they will cruise through the finals to claim the premiership.

Advertisement

“Finals footy is a different breed,” Kelly said. “I think you can go all the way through, build consistency, be undefeated, but then we’ve obviously bowed out twice in a semi-final and then had that heartbreak of losing a grand final. “It’s finals footy, everyone steps up, the game goes to a new level. I think we’ve seen it in the NRL this week with the games just played, and some of those games were insane.” The Titans have been responsible for some Roosters heartbreak in the past. Gold Coast won a gritty semi-final 12-0 in 2023, but lost to Newcastle in the grand final. The Gold Coast are certainly capable of causing an upset again this year. “They’ve been so good; they’ve been unreal,” Kelly said of the Titans.

Advertisement

“I think they’re one of the hot contenders, to be honest, to be in that grand final, and I think they deserve to have the week off, same as us, because of the form they’ve been in.” Titans captain Georgia Hale and Roosters counterpart Isabelle Kelly. Oscar Colman Titans captain Georgia Hale – who was part of the team that lost that 2023 grand final – has total belief in her team. Not only are they battle-hardened, she said, after defeating every other finals team in the regular season – Broncos, Tigers, Knights and Raiders – but they are also capable of turning the tables on the Roosters in the decider. “Absolutely [we can beat them]. The belief is there, and gosh, that would be such a good feeling,” Hale said.

Advertisement

“To be the best, you want to beat the best. So yeah, just say when and where.” After 15 years, the Tigers are playing in the finals again It’s been 15 long years, but the Wests Tigers are finally playing finals football again. For the first time since 2011, a top-grade Tigers team will play a match at the business end of the season, thanks to the club’s NRLW side sealing a top-four finish with a 7-4 record during the 11-match regular season. Wests Tigers captain Kezie Apps has been with the team since their inaugural year in 2022. George Chan

Advertisement

It’s an impressive turnaround for a team that finished with just one win, and the wooden spoon for the second year in a row in 2025. The last Wests Tigers team to play finals was Tim Sheens’ 2011 squad that included Benji Marshall, Lote Tuqiri and Robbie Farah. One of the most significant changes for the NRLW team this year has been the arrival of coach Craig Sandercock. “If you were to say to me at the start of the year, you’re playing finals footy, I would have 100 per cent taken that,” Sandercock said. “It’s been a great, great year, and you could probably consider it a really successful year from the club, especially with where we’ve come from.”

Advertisement

The team always had potential, said Sandercock, but there were a handful of areas that required improvement. “When I watched all their games from last year, they only won one game, but there were periods in every game that they competed, and they competed hard, and it was just, I suppose, some key moments last year that really cost them,” Sandercock said. “Then that fed into that mindset of, here we go again, and then they concede another try and another try. So, for us, it was all about trying to build some resilience and really work hard on icing or winning those key moments in games that can lead to positive results.” Wests Tigers NRLW coach Craig Sandercock. NRL Images The recruitment of veteran players Raecene McGregor and Shaylee Bent has also been a huge boost, and those experienced players have joined forces with captain Kezie Apps and forward Sarah Togatuki – who have been with the club since that first 2023 season – to steer the team into the finals.

Advertisement

“I feel like this year the coach and the recruitment [team] have done a great job of finding that balance [between youth an experience],” said Apps. “We’ve still got our young girls coming through who are learning and who are going really good, but we’ve also got that great balance of the leaders and the experience within the group as well. Related Article NRL 2026 The Dolphins are one win from a grand final. They should thank Spencer Leniu “It’s obviously been a big change this year from going from only winning one game last year, and now here we are near finals, and we’ve come fourth. “Reflecting on the season that we’ve had ... and comparing that to last year coming last and then coming fourth, I think that’s something that needs to be celebrated and something that needs to be recognised of how hard the girls have worked to get to where we are.” The Tigers will play Canberra, who they lost 22-10 to in the final round of the season, in week one of the finals.

SportRugby UnionReds ‘Crazy couple of years’: How freakish Warriors flyer ended up playing rugby for the Reds Nick Wright September 16, 2026 — 2:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As the New Zealand Warriors attempt to keep their NRL season alive and avenge their qualifying final defeat to the Dolphins, one of the most enigmatic try-scorers in the club’s history will launch a new chapter in a rival code. David Fusitu’a has been quietly plying his trade in rugby union, far removed from the spotlight, having made the move to Brisbane, where he has spent two seasons with Brothers, winning the Hospital Cup premiership this year in the process. Now he has been called into the Queensland Reds’ fold for their forthcoming Super Rugby Australia clash with the New South Wales Waratahs. David Fusitu’a (pictured on the left in his Warriors days, and on the right with the Reds) will make his comeback to top-flight sport with the Queensland Reds this weekend. Getty/Reds Media The 31-year-old 106-kilogram flyer played 106 games for the Warriors – scoring 61 tries, many with some freakish, air-defying finishes – before departing for the English Super League for three years with Leeds Rhinos. He also managed nine Test caps for Tonga and two for New Zealand.

Advertisement

Fusitu’a admits that when he drew the curtain on his England venture, he felt he still had something to offer on the field. Eager to give the 15-man game a try, he consulted a friend in New Zealand, who linked him up with Brothers. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow But while a comeback to professional football full-time was not on his radar for now, Fusitu’a was quick to answer a “surprise” SOS from new Reds coach Vern Cotter, and will line up at outside-centre for his new side at the Santos Festival of Rugby in Roma this weekend. “It’s been a crazy couple of years,” Fusitu’a said. “I finished up in England with Leeds Rhinos and moved back to this side of the world. I knew I wanted to give rugby a crack, and just by chance, I ended up here in Brisbane. “It’s obviously a weird time when you’re adjusting to life after professional rugby, and I would always think to myself during rugby, ‘Is there something else I’m passionate about outside rugby?’

Advertisement

“I’ve found it in youth work lately, and have enjoyed giving back to kids in need, but also spending a bit more time with the family and being able to give back to them.” Fusitu’a will be joined in the Reds’ squad by former Wallabies flyer Sefa Naivalu, as Cotter ushers in reinforcements to cover injuries to Izaia Perese (calf), Josh Flook (torn achilles), and Lachie Anderson (facial fracture) in the aftermath of the club’s 29-28 defeat to the Western Force. Loading But even with a new challenge ahead of him, Fusitu’a could not resist looking towards what awaits his old Warriors teammates on Sunday night, when they square off in an elimination semi-final against Newcastle at Eden Park. New Zealand had the chance to lock in a preliminary final last weekend, after they led 16-8 deep into the second half, only to succumb to a Herbie Farnworth-inspired Dolphins comeback.

Advertisement

Related Article NRL 2026 Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs “It definitely wasn’t the result I’m sure the boys were wanting, and us fans, but they get another chance. I’m a big Warriors supporter, I obviously played there and am still a big supporter of the boys and have a good few mates who are running around there,” Fusitu’a said. “Players like Chanel Harris-Tavita are still running around. He was still quite young at the time when I was there, but he’s come through the system, and it’ll be very special for him. “They’ve still got to get the job done, but I have big belief in that squad and what they’re building.” The Reds’ looming match will be the first time this year five-eighth Tom Lynagh will play back-to-back games, after a hamstring issue and illness limited him to barely 18 minutes of Super Rugby in 2026.

Advertisement

title: Pendlebury move causes free agency compensation shock for Hawks, Suns

SportAFLAFL 2026 Pendlebury move causes free agency compensation shock for Hawks, Suns Michael Gleeson September 16, 2026 — 2:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collingwood champion Scott Pendlebury’s move to the Gold Coast as a free agent is likely to dilute the compensation the Suns would receive for losing Ben King, complicating the coveted spearhead’s planned move to Hawthorn. The Suns and Hawks were stunned to discover that if the AFL’s games record holder and oldest player moved as a free agent to the Gold Coast that it would potentially impact the compensation the club would receive for losing King. Scott Pendlebury of the Magpies and Massimo D’Ambrosio of the Hawks contest the ball. Getty Images It had been assumed that at Pendlebury’s age - he turns 39 in January - his move would not draw compensation for Collingwood, nor affect compensation for the Suns if King left as a free agent. King is yet to formally declare Hawthorn as his preferred destination but has told the Suns he wants to leave as a free agent to return to Victoria.

Advertisement

Hawthorn have been hoping that the Suns would not match contract terms for the restricted free agent and accept the expected compensation pick at selection seven in the draft. Pendlebury coming in as a free agent could push any King compensation back to an end of first round draft pick. Loading If there was a risk of the compensation for King being pushed back to an end of first round pick because of Pendlebury’s arrival, the Suns would be likely to match the contract terms and force Hawthorn into a trade for King. Having to trade for King would then impact the Hawks’ ability to trade for Zach Merrett from Essendon, who is expected to again ask for a trade to Hawthorn this year.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The ‘Butters rule’ the AFL should introduce to fix a shonky system Free agency compensation is determined based on the net result of free agents entering and leaving the club. Clubs are not formally told in advance what compensation pick they would receive from free agents coming in and out and the AFL formula for deciding compensation is deliberately kept confidential. The Pendlebury position is academic for now as no contract terms have been lodged with the AFL for either Pendlebury or King, in order for the league to officially decide on compensation, but the clubs have been warned that the veteran’s age is only one of three factors to consider in free agency. The amount and length of the contract is just as important. Above the age of 31, it doesn’t matter how old a player is as far as free agency compensation is concerned. To preserve their potential compensation for King, Pendlebury and the Suns could ask Collingwood to delist him. That way he could go to the Suns as a delisted free agent.

Advertisement

Delisted free agents do not draw compensation. Collingwood, however, have been reluctant to delist Pendlebury, being uncomfortable with the idea of delisting the club’s greatest ever player. Zach Merrett is likely to request a trade to Hawthorn again. Getty Images The Suns and Collingwood could also do a minor trade for the former captain and two time premiership player. Such an arrangement occurred when former Hawthorn premiership captain Sam Mitchell moved to West Coast at the end of his career. Like Pendlebury’s move to the Suns, it was part of a transition plan into coaching after a brief playing period.

text:

Updated BusinessCompaniesOnline gambling Gambling company let more than 150 problem gamblers stay on platform Elias Visontay Updated September 16, 2026 — 1:52pm ,first published September 16, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dabble, a social media-linked betting platform, has been slapped with more than $1 million in penalties after it breached self-exclusion laws, kept the accounts of more than 150 problem gamblers open and sent marketing material to them more than 800 times. The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) on Wednesday announced its investigation into the wagering platform – that allows users to copy bets from friends, former sports stars or other personalities – found a range of breaches of national self-exclusion laws known as BetStop. Dabble was fined more than $1 million for breaching self-exclusion laws. iStock The ACMA said Dabble, for which betting giant Tabcorp paid $33 million for a 20 per cent stake in 2022, failed to close 157 wagering accounts after the account holders registered with BetStop. The betting platform founded in 2020 and known for its sponsorship of the National Basketball League and Supercars Championship, also sent 165 self-excluded people a total of 839 electronic messages as either SMS, emails or app push notifications, the ACMA found.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Online gambling $6b betting giant had 500 problem-gambling breaches, but the regulator took too long to fine it BetStop was launched in 2023 as part of Australia’s self-exclusion laws aimed at allowing gamblers fearing or fighting addiction to have all of their accounts closed. Operators must also cease sending them marketing. Additionally, signing up to BetStop bans an individual from opening a new account with any platform licensed to operate in Australia. Wagering companies are obliged to inform customers about BetStop in any electronic messages promoting or advertising gambling. The ACMA also found Dabble sent 45 customers more than 2000 push notifications without including information about BetStop, in breach of the laws. Dabble, which is led by former PointsBet and CrownBet executive Tom Rundle as CEO, posted a $14.4 million profit in 2025. ACMA member Carolyn Lidgerwood said “these were serious breaches by Dabble” which had the potential to cause real harm.

Advertisement

“People who register with BetStop have made a clear decision to exclude themselves from online wagering,” she said. “Providers must respect that decision by closing their accounts promptly and ensuring they are not targeted with gambling promotions.” “BetStop is an important consumer protection measure, but it only works if wagering companies follow the rules,” Lidgerwood said. The $1.069 million in penalties Dabble has now paid were part of a two-year court-enforceable undertaking, requiring the company to conduct an independent review of its compliance systems and make the investment required to implement recommended improvements. “If Dabble breaches its undertaking, the ACMA can take the company to court to enforce terms,” the regulator said. When this masthead contacted Dabble’s publicly available email address for comment, its automated chatbot ROGER referred media inquiries to its public relations team. When asked for that email address, ROGER said: “We don’t have a publicly listed communications or public relations contact available for media inquiries.”

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Ladbrokes warns customers: gamble, or have accounts depleted ROGER said Dabble’s only published contact details were a physical mailing address for its headquarters based in Darwin. Gambling industry critics have suggested that companies are drawn to register in the Northern Territory due to favourable tax and regulations. After this story was first published, a Dabble spokesperson sent this masthead a statement which said the company “regret(s) that these contraventions occurred and take responsibility for instances where our internal BetStop controls did not perform as intended”. “Dabble confirms the ACMA’s investigation found no accounts were able to be accessed, and no bets were placed by Betstop registered customers. However, we recognise the overriding importance of meeting our responsible gambling and regulatory obligations and have strengthened our controls to reduce the risk of this occurring again,” the spokesperson said. The ACMA has previously come under fire for taking so long to conduct its investigations that it missed the 12-month window in which it could issue a penalty. Changes coming into effect next year extend the window to 24 months, and increase the maximum penalties for each breach of the rules. title: Barkly jags rich rare earths across 23km in NT
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Barkly jags rich rare earths across 23km in NT Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 16, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In what can only be described as a stellar assay-results debut, Barkly Rare Earths has hit significant rare earths mineralisation in every one of the first 28 holes assayed from a maiden drilling campaign at its flagship Barkly project in the Northern Territory. Results from the company’s 10,000-metre phase one resource expansion program have confirmed a massive, shallow, flat-lying mineralised system, with significant intercepts returned from holes drilled up to 23 kilometres apart, flagging the system’s huge potential size. A reverse circulation drill rig in action at Barkly Rare Earths’ maiden drilling campaign in the Northern Territory. The campaign is geared towards testing extensions to Barkly’s existing 40-million-tonne inferred mineral resource, which grades 2100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). Based on these first numbers, it appears to be well on its way. Intriguingly, the current resource is largely split between northern and southern deposits, leaving almost 15km of virtually untouched ground in between for the drill bit to put to the truth detector. That sizeable gap helps explain Barkly’s lofty exploration target of 200 million to one billion tonnes grading between 1600ppm and 1900ppm TREO. Highlights from the first batch of assays include a 2-metre hit grading 2716 ppm TREO from just 11m, featuring a higher-grade 0.5-metre core assaying an impressive 6064 ppm TREO. Another hole returned a 1.5-metre section grading 3228 ppm TREO from 15m, including a 0.5-metre interval at a solid 5170 ppm TREO.

Advertisement

‘Our ambition is to define a large-scale, high-grade resource.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Notably, the mineralisation is not only high-grade but also rich in the valuable magnet rare earth oxides (MREO), which currently make up 34 per cent of the company’s inferred mineral resource of TREO. The MREO include yttrium, neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, some of the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are essential for manufacturing high-strength permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. In a stunning outcome, MREO made up a consistently high 31 to 40 per cent of the TREO in 27 of the 28 fresh intercepts. The project itself is no run-of-the-mill sediment-hosted rare earths play, with mineralisation stretching through laterally extensive, near-horizontal Cretaceous sandstones and unusually tied to aluminium-phosphate-sulphate (APS) minerals. Adding to the project’s appeal, the mineralisation starts at shallow depths, from as little as 3m below surface in some areas, pointing towards the potential for a simple, low-cost open pit mining operation. Furthermore, the company says concentrations of the deleterious radioactive elements uranium and thorium are consistently low, a significant advantage for processing and a key feature that distinguishes it from many hard rock rare earth deposits.

Advertisement

Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “Twenty-eight holes assayed and twenty-eight intercepts — that is a very satisfying result, and the holes 23 km apart look like the same flat-lying horizon we mapped. Our ambition is to define a large-scale, high-grade resource, and results like these are why we are drilling another 300-plus holes.” The company recently announced a stunning 99 per cent extraction of high-value MREO from a single-stage metallurgical test on material from its namesake project. The result was achieved using a simple initial caustic conversion followed by a hydrochloric acid leach. Importantly, the test separated 92 per cent of the phosphorus impurities into the caustic solution, with no measurable rare earths detected, marking a significant technical win that could simplify and reduce the cost of downstream purification. Barkly only listed on the ASX in January this year following an oversubscribed $8 million IPO. The company is now furiously drilling to deliver an updated mineral resource estimate by the end of the year. The results come at a time when Western nations are scrambling to secure their own supplies of critical minerals and reduce their reliance on China. Beijing recently tightened its grip on the market by placing export controls on several key heavy rare earths, creating a perfect storm for explorers such as Barkly, as it chases what could emerge as a potentially globally significant deposit outside of China.

Advertisement

Barkly has drilled 68 holes to date, with assays from the first 28 now in. Samples from another 30 holes are currently at the laboratory, with a continuous flow of results expected through the final quarter of the year. The company plans to drill a further 300-plus holes to continue probing the extent of what appears to be a massive mineralised system. With a 100 per cent strike rate from the get-go, a mineralised footprint that already stretches for tens of kilometres and the all-important magnet metals showing up in spades, Barkly has certainly hit the ground running. With hundreds more drill holes planned and assays from dozens more already in the lab, the company should be providing plenty of news flow to keep the market interested. If these early numbers are a sign of things to come, Barkly’s Northern Territory story could get interesting very quickly. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? title: The 31-year-old who might end up as the world’s most educated person
text:
Advertisement

BusinessEntrepreneurshipEducation The 31-year-old who might end up as the world’s most educated person Scott Cacciola September 16, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Early in the autumn semester of the 2025-26 academic year, Lisa Belkin, an adjunct professor at Columbia University’s journalism school, realised that one of her students, Jamie Beaton, had yet to show up for class. Belkin, who avoids combing the internet for information about her students, knew nothing about Beaton. She was curious about his absence, though, so she reached out to a dean, who sent an email. Jamie Beaton is hungry for degrees. NYT Beaton was apologetic in his reply, saying he had mixed up his schedule. He was in New Zealand, teaching a course in entrepreneurship at the University of Auckland, but would be back in New York the next week. That was when Belkin decided to break her rule. Who was this guy?

Advertisement

Beaton, she learned, had graduated magna cum laude from Harvard University in 2016, picking up a master’s degree in applied mathematics along the way. He had gone on to collect an MBA from Stanford University. Then a law degree from Yale University. That was followed by a doctor of philosophy in public policy from Oxford, where he was a Rhodes scholar – all before age 28. Related Article Medicine She lost her sight. Her Wall Street billionaire father bet on a daring new treatment Attending classes remotely and in person, he earned additional master’s degrees from – deep breath – the University of Pennsylvania (education entrepreneurship), Stanford (education technology), Princeton University (finance), Cornell University (healthcare policy and economics), Dartmouth College (implementation science), King’s College London (war studies) and Tsinghua University in Beijing (global affairs). Still, there was more: Beaton, who was born and raised in New Zealand, was a founder and the chief executive of Crimson Education, a college admissions counselling service that has been valued at more than $US600 million ($840 million). A week after his apologetic reply, Beaton made his first appearance in Belkin’s classroom. As the semester went on, he did not miss an assignment.

Advertisement

“He was a joy to get to know,” Belkin said. “But it was also the weirdest relationship I’ve ever had with a student.” ‘Passions and curiosities’ A 168-centimetres-tall personification of naked ambition whose LinkedIn profile has been the subject of memes and Reddit threads, Beaton has gone to the head of a rarefied class – perpetual students. In his final year of high school, Beaton took more than twice the number of required courses. He was admitted to 25 universities, including Harvard, Yale and Princeton. AP If he continues collecting advanced degrees at such a swift pace, he will surpass Benjamin B. Bolger, who has racked up 16 at age 50. He might even beat Michael Nicholson, an octogenarian forever scholar with more than 30 degrees to his name.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Billionaires Billionaire’s $6.3m ‘bride price’ stunt could backfire Away from his studies, Beaton, 31, has become a player in the field of college admissions counselling. His clients pay between $US30,000 and $US200,000 for a multiyear program designed to enhance their children’s chances of getting into top universities. His own academic background has raised some questions, starting with: How can this be real? Is it education as performance art? An elaborate marketing ploy for his business? The truth, Beaton said, is more prosaic. “The first five degrees had a clear skill acquisition component to them,” he said. “Since then, it’s really been about following different passions and curiosities.”

Advertisement

We met on a recent afternoon in Manhattan, not far from where he lives with his wife, Priscilla Beaton. His day was crowded with appointments, including an evening event at the Harvard Club in Midtown, where he and his Crimson Education colleagues would hold a meet-and-greet with potential clients. “I love the action, and I love a jam-packed day,” he said. “It’s good fun.” So many things are, according to Beaton, “good fun”. An abridged list: helping students decode the college admissions process. Studying the viability of distressed companies. Grabbing snacks in the Amtrak cafe car. Reading big books in one gulp. Riding the fastest roller coaster in the world on a recent trip to Saudi Arabia. He was cheerful and accommodating. He spoke rapidly, in fully formed paragraphs. Shortly before we met, he emailed me a 61-page legal notice stating that Crimson Education had initiated a $US28 million hostile takeover of Kip McGrath, an international tutoring provider. He keeps up with his studies even while travelling the world on business. A few weeks ago, he was in India when he submitted his end-of-semester project for a course at Brown University, where he is working toward a master’s in data science. He said he tries to get six hours of sleep a night.

Advertisement

“Oh, he’s lying,” John Key, a former prime minister of New Zealand, said in a telephone interview. Key, the chair of Crimson Education, considers Beaton the second-brightest New Zealander, behind the noted scientist Ernest Rutherford, who died nearly 90 years ago. “And I’m only saying that because it’s hard to take it away from the guy who split the atom,” Key said. Beaton has amassed quite a collection of college T-shirts. NYT Amy Chua, the author of Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother, a 2011 memoir about her hard-driving parenting style, was one of Beaton’s professors at Yale Law School. In recent years she has written more letters of recommendation for him than she can count.

Advertisement

“He can’t stop applying to things,” she said. She acknowledged that his story sounds apocryphal. “Jamie is so unusual that I wouldn’t have been surprised if someone had said to me, ‘Oh, he invented the whole thing – he doesn’t even have a mother’,” Chua said. ‘I want to work’ The making of the boy who wanted to know everything began in Auckland, New Zealand, where he was the only child of a single mother, Paula Beaton. She was pregnant when she and Jamie’s father separated, she said. They later divorced.

Advertisement

Jamie, who took his mother’s surname, recalled “odd experiences” when he was young, like when his mother joined him for father-son breakfasts at his primary school. But family was important – his maternal grandparents, John and Sarah Beaton, lived with them – and so was education. Jamie’s grandfather, a tradesman, always seemed to be leafing through a newspaper or an Andy McNab thriller. Related Article Billionaires The family feud over the $65 billion Ray-Ban fortune “Academics was our religion,” Jamie said. His mother said that one of her goals had been to expose her son to myriad opportunities. So he played tennis and basketball. He went camping, swimming, kayaking. He was nine when his mother introduced him to a chess coach named Glenn Harry Kwok. Kwok and Paula soon began dating and are now long-term partners. “I wondered why we weren’t doing much chess,” Jamie said.

Advertisement

His mother chauffeured him to tutoring centres and hired academic coaches, which was unusual for a middle-class family in New Zealand. “We wouldn’t be getting new cars or anything like that,” Paula Beaton said. “Everything revolved around education, and we didn’t see it as a sacrifice.” As a teenager, Jamie dreamed of attending a top college in the United States. In his final year of high school, he took more than twice the number of required courses. He was admitted to 25 universities, including Harvard, Yale and Princeton. Beaton and wife Priscilla are based in New York. NYT Before leaving home, he co-founded the counselling service that would become Crimson Education, billing it as a way to help international students navigate their way to US universities. After all, he had done it himself.

Advertisement

At Harvard, he felt all alone at first. Then he joined 15 student organisations, including the debate club and the undergraduate economics association. Brett Davis, one of Beaton’s roommates at Harvard, grew accustomed to his 2am business calls. “That was certainly a clue that this guy was thinking beyond the script of what is normal to do or achieve in college,” Davis said. Beaton was a sophomore when he emailed Julian Robertson, the founder of Tiger Management, a Wall Street hedge fund. Following a practice he had used with other traders at his firm, Robertson sent him off to be evaluated by a psychoanalyst – “Good fun,” Beaton said – before bringing him on board. Between classes at Harvard, Beaton spent two days a week at the Tiger Management offices in New York. Robertson, who died in 2022, and his son Alex, who now runs the firm, became mentors. Tiger Management was an early investor in Crimson Education. Alex Robertson recalled urging Beaton to have more work-life balance: Why not spend a week in Cancun with his buddies? “Honestly, Alex,” Beaton told him, “I can’t think of anything worse than sitting on a beach for five days when I want to work.”

Advertisement

Beaton was among the dozens of students who took a class on entrepreneurship taught by David Ager, a senior lecturer at Harvard Business School. Beaton stood out, not only because of his prominent spot in the amphitheatre – “In the front, three rows up,” Ager said – but also because he was such an active participant. Related Article Opinion

Billionaires The billionaire brat pack can’t stop whingeing. They’re only embarrassing themselves Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor “I say this with love,” Ager said, “but I’m sure there was a little bit of frustration that he had to share the time with other people.” Throughout his journey, Beaton has juggled academics and business. Belkin recalled that he often had his laptop open during class to check work emails or his stock portfolio. “Yet everything came in on time,” Belkin said. Beaton was multitasking in other ways, too, often talking with the student seated next to him, Priscilla Putzer. “There was a lot of whispering and giggling,” Belkin said.

Advertisement

Beaton and Putzer were married in April at a ceremony on the beach in Santa Monica, California. A company grows Crimson Education has not been immune from criticism. Early on, it faced pushback for using aggressive sales tactics and employing many college students as tutors and counsellors. As the company grew, Beaton said, it shifted to employing more full-time counsellors – the company now has 1200 full-time staff members, he said – and hired an accounting firm to vet its numbers. Of the 10,000 students who have used its services, more than 2000 have been accepted by Ivy League universities, Stanford or the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, he said. The company has also found itself the subject of a broader critique – that its high price tag effectively self-selects students who already have a good chance of getting into elite universities.

Advertisement

Jeff Selingo, a journalist who has written several books about college admissions, said that private counsellors can be a helpful resource for those who can afford them. “But it’s not going to get you into a place that you can’t get into otherwise,” he said. “I love the action, and I love a jam-packed day. It’s good fun.” Jamie Beaton Hamish Coates, an education expert at the Australian National University and Beaton’s thesis adviser at Tsinghua University, praised Beaton as someone who understood “the power of higher education”. But Coates posed a hypothetical: “Do you really want your child to be grooming themselves for the Ivy League from the age of five, when 95 per cent fail to get in? Or are you better off doing some finger painting, reading Frog and Toad and having a good life?” Beaton has heard that argument before – the “pressure-cooker environment” on one side and the “chill, happy childhood” on the other. He doesn’t buy the premise. “The students who try harder in high school are often the happiest and most engaged,” he said. His own future appears to be a work in progress. For now, he said, he is focused on “education and entrepreneurship”, along with starting a family. But several of his friends said they could see him entering politics. He has worked with New Zealand’s centre-right National Party, which was once headed by Key.

Advertisement

“If you said to me, ‘In 35 years’ time, Jamie will still be the CEO of Crimson’, I don’t see it,” Key said. “I think he’s got other, bigger things that he’s going to move on to.” Related Article Putin's Russia Billionaire gives Moscow the middle finger after being placed on Russia’s most wanted list At the end of his busy day, Beaton and his Crimson Education colleagues met with teenagers and their parents in a wood-paneled room of the Harvard Club. As servers passed around hors d’oeuvres, he stood before the group as a living advertisement for his company, the one-time whiz kid who had beaten the system. At one point Beaton ceded the stage to a colleague who spoke about scholarships available to high school students, including the John Locke essay competition. “How many are familiar with John Locke?” she asked.

Advertisement

A single hand shot up from the front row. “Not you, Jamie,” she said. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

title: Joyous energy and raucous humour collide in this five-star gig
text:

Key points MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian return to the Palais with If You’re Feeling Sinister

MUSIC: Cellist Pieter Wispelwey explores solo suites by Benjamin Britten

DANCE: Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring One Last Tree to La Mama

OPERA: Lyric Opera put on a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE: 7 Dances for 7 People is performed at Northcote Town Hall

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.

Advertisement

As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

MUSIC

Pieter Wispelwey with Piers Lane ★★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15 Pure genius. These two words arguably encapsulate the astonishing imagination behind the three solo suites that Benjamin Britten composed for the Russian cellist Mstislav Rostropovich between 1964 and 1971. Taking Bach’s fabled cello suites as a model, these tours de force remain revolutionary in pushing the instrument’s boundaries of timbre and texture. Pieter Wispelwey performs at Melbourne Recital Centre, September 15, 2026 Laura Manariti Over three evenings, Dutch cellist Pieter Wispelwey, long an ardent and persuasive exponent of these works, is performing programs centred around each suite. Prokofiev and Shostakovich were appropriate stablemates in the series opener, not least because Prokofiev wrote his Cello Sonata in C, Op. 119 for Rostropovich, but also that the cellist was part of the deep friendship and admiration shared between himself, Shostakovich and Britten.

Advertisement

Providing the first taste of Wispelwey’s chameleonic way with his 1760 Guadagnini cello, the Prokofiev ran the gamut of emotions, starting with its dark, sombre opening before flowering into rich lyricism, moments of childlike wonder and folkloric exuberance. Britten’s Cello Suite No. 1, Op. 72 was full of ear-bending marvels, including a witty, cleverly constructed fugue and an evocative march in which the masterly bouncing of the bow summoned up martial images. A stunning moto perpetuo led to the return of the imposing, unifying Canto. Few others would be capable of bringing this music alive so vibrantly and comprehensibly. Pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic Laura Manariti Wispelwey ensured Shostakovich’s Cello Sonata in D minor, Op. 40 brimmed over with fascinating detail; bringing richly burnished tone to the eerie opening melody and plaintive Largo, unerring technique to the manic second movement and cheeky playfulness to the finale. Here and in the Prokofiev, pianist Piers Lane’s committed partnership was entirely empathetic. Setting aside the substandard printed program that doesn’t even list the movements of the works performed, don’t miss the remaining two opportunities to hear astounding music performed by musicians of genius.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

DANCE

Our Last Tree ★★★

La Mama, until September 18 Hobart’s Nelipot Collective bring something we rarely see on Melbourne stages: unpretentiously referential contemporary dance. Their latest show, Our Last Tree, points us with a sort of guileless enthusiasm towards the green earth and its wonders. Nelipot Collective perform Our Last Tree as part of La Mama’s Hope Punk Climate Festival Darren Gill Sometimes the relentless self-reflexivity of our local choreographers – their unwillingness to make work about the world beyond the stage – can seem like a fear of artistic failure. Nelipot embrace that fear with an earnest, wilfully naive fable of loss and recovery. Certainly, their slightly manic smiles and touchy-feely involvement of the audience suggest a community-oriented performance. You can imagine them at a farmers’ market, amid haybales and squealing children munching on small-batch fudge.

Advertisement

And yet I find their evocation of the life of the forest compelling. What they do best here is suggest – with reaching, serpentine limbs – the way that forests envelop us completely, above and below and all around. The intimate stage at La Mama, further compressed by the placement of a cardboard tree along one side, suits these densely convolved bodies. They seem to fill the space completely, coiling themselves into any chink of vacancy. Composer and violist Andrea Breen accompanies the performance with catchy, rather grand melodic hooks, which she returns to between wandering passages. Her music suggests something rooted yet inexorably moving, a tree’s stillness alive with change. Her score also implies a fuller orchestration: I hear the ghosts of horns and oboes underneath it. And yet the exposed solo voice suggests kinship with the last tree. Haunting, effective and beautifully played. Other production elements are less impressive. The slime-green tulle and the cardboard trunk (endearingly ornamented with hand-drawn growth rings) suggest a production for children; I suspect a younger audience would respond well. Yes, the work could be called unsophisticated, but only if that also means a refreshing independence from convention, as well as the courage to approach their subject directly.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.

Advertisement

Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.

Advertisement

After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Arts Second strike planned by Arts Centre Melbourne employees The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

title: 'Not possible to know' if lottery pact was best deal
text:
An independent auditor isn't certain a state squeezed every cent out of selling its exclusive public lottery licence rights for four decades by not fielding rival bids.

The Victorian Auditor-General's Office on Wednesday released its report into the state government's $1.145 billion, 40-year licence deal with The Lottery Corporation, announced in May.

Victoria's previous 10-year deal with the ASX-listed company, which also has 40-year lottery agreements with NSW, South Australia and the NT along with a 65-year deal with Queensland, had been due to expire in 2028.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The licence extension until 2068 was revealed to the stock market on May 5, the same day the Victorian budget was handed down, and followed exclusive negotiations between the parties.

Enver Erdogan says the process delivered the best return of a licence extension in Australia. (James Ross/AAP PHOTOS)

The watchdog found the Victorian government had "sound reasons" for excluding other operators as a competitive process was "unlikely" to deliver a better outcome.

"The agreed premium exceeded the reserve price set by the government," the report said.

In November 2023, the company sent the treasurer and minister an initial proposal to extend the licence by 20 to 40 years in return for a "material up-front payment".

The Victorian government subsequently passed laws to allow backroom negotiations on the lottery licence between the relevant minister and an "invited" applicant.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The government's commercial adviser estimated a theoretical value for the licence of about $1.372 billion.

But the auditor-general cautioned against comparing the final premium with the modelled value as it was subject to inherent uncertainty and a range of assumptions, including discount rates.

"While agencies sought to maximise value within a bilateral framework, it is not possible to know with certainty whether a higher premium could have been achieved under an alternative approach," the report said.

The Victorian budget projected a net operating surplus of $1.05 billion in 2026/27, with state net debt forecast to top $199.3 billion by 2030.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The terms of the deal required the company to pay $1.145 billion to the government in two instalments in 2026/27.

"The up-front payment will improve the state's short-term net debt position and net operating cash flow in the year received," the report said.

The auditor-general did not find any significant probity issues but said the government's approach limited public transparency.

The licence extension was announced the same day Victoria's annual budget was released. (Joel Carrett/AAP PHOTOS)

The state's gaming minister, Enver Erdogan, said the process delivered the best return of a licence extension in Australian history.

"The report is clear - this process was conducted properly," he said.

The Victorian opposition continued to maintain Labor changed the rules and kept Victorians in the dark in a "vain attempt" to keep net debt under $200 billion.

"Victorians deserve better than a government that taxes them in secret and signs up to secret deals behind closed doors," an opposition spokesman said.
